speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The Land Transport and Related Matters Bill is an omnibus Bill that regularises provisions across several existing Acts.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: It is also a joint Bill by the Ministry of Transport (MOT) and the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) covering several key areas.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I will speak on amendments pertaining to the Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) 2.0 system and increasing penalties for serious vehicular offences.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Minister of State Baey Yam Keng will introduce amendments related to active mobility, including regulations on personal mobility aids (PMAs), and the keeping of unsafe personal mobility devices (PMDs).

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will address the MHA components of this Bill, including penalties for speed limiter offences.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The transition to ERP 2.0 has been discussed extensively in this House before.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But let me recap quickly why we need ERP 2.0 and the benefits that it will bring.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The current ERP system has been in place since 1998.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: In combination with vehicle ownership policies, road pricing has kept traffic congestion in check during the peak hours.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: However, after almost three decades, the current ERP system is reaching its end of life.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Replacing obsolete components and infrastructure had become unsustainably challenging and expensive.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Hence, in 2013, we decided to prepare to move to a new ERP 2.0 system using Global Navigation Satellite System technology.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: While ERP 2.0 was intended to be a step up, providing useful features for motorists such as real-time traffic information, it was nevertheless based on prevailing technology in 2013.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The implementation of ERP 2.0 took longer than initially planned.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Some features envisioned for the On-Board Unit (OBU), such as displaying charging information and traffic alerts, can now also be done via other means, for example, on smartphones.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Nevertheless, the ERP 2.0 design, with an OBU, remained fit for purpose for accurate and efficient road charging.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Since we first began the OBU installation exercise in 2024, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) has received much feedback.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: LTA has taken the feedback on board and this has helped to improve the user experience.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For instance, after feedback, vehicle owners were given the option to choose not to have a display screen, which would be more similar to the ERP 1.0 experience.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: But I note that in the end, the vast majority of car owners chose to install display screens.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: To date, more than 90% of vehicles have the OBU installed.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And having tried out the new OBU, more motorists have now given positive feedback.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Motorists tell us that they find some features useful, such as car park availability, reminders on speed limits and bus lanes in operation.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We have been introducing these and other new features progressively.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Since September last year, motorists can use the OBU to pay for missed ERP charges by simply clicking a button.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Compared to ERP 1.0, ERP 2.0 will be more precise and finer in targeting road congestion.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: It allows us to introduce new charging points without the need for expensive and large physical gantries.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: We can also spread out ERP charges in smaller amounts across several locations as opposed to just one location and this will be fairer.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: At this point, let me reassure motorists that we will be judicious in adding new charging points, doing so only when needed at persistent congestion hotspots.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Distance-based charging is something that we will continue to study and explore after motorists have gotten more used to the new system and the situation is more stable.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I want to thank the 93% of vehicle owners who have already installed the OBU.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For the remaining ones, LTA is issuing a final reminder.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: These vehicle owners, who have already been previously notified, will have another three months to install their OBUs at no cost.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: So, I strongly encourage the remaining vehicle owners who are holding out to install their OBUs as soon as possible.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This is because ERP 2.0 uses satellite technology, rather than gantries, to determine the vehicle's location for charging.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Clause 65 of the Bill amends the Road Traffic Act 1961 to allow for this.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For foreign-registered private vehicles, we encourage them to install OBUs for usage-based charging, although we recognise that occasional visitors may prefer not to do so.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Vehicles without OBUs can still pay a daily flat fee, like cars without the In-vehicle Unit (IU) today.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Malaysian taxis, however, will be required to install the OBU, as this is necessary for us to track and enforce against such vehicles if needed within Singapore.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: And these will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For serious cases of deliberate non-compliance or misuse, the legislation provides for penalties of up to $20,000 and/or imprisonment of up to two years.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This Bill also covers housekeeping amendments that harmonise penalties for two categories of vehicular offences.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: For non-individuals, first time offenders can be fined up to $40,000, and up to $80,000 for repeat offenders.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Another serious vehicular offence is keeping or using of unregistered or deregistered vehicles.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: These enhanced penalties are necessary as we are seeing a growing trend of unregistered vehicles on our roads.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Some of them are used for criminal activities, such as drug trafficking.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: These vehicles also pose serious road safety risks, as they operate without valid insurance or inspections, and are often involved in hit-and-run accidents.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Going forward, ERP 2.0 will also make it easier to detect and enforce against such vehicles.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This Bill also includes a few supporting amendments.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Clauses 46 and 47 will amend the Land Transport Authority of Singapore Act to expressly empower the LTA to grant financial incentives, support, grant, aid or assistance.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: This gives flexibility for potential future schemes where direct disbursement may be necessary.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: Clauses 48 to 50 will amend the Parking Places Act to enable prosecution in the case of inaccurate lodgements.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: The provisions in the Bill support the transition to ERP 2.0 and harmonise vehicular offence penalties across our regulatory system.

speaker: The Acting Minister for Transport (Mr Jeffrey Siow)
text: I will now invite Minister of State for Transport to elaborate on the active mobility measures in this Bill, followed by Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs who will elaborate on the measures under MHA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: First, the Bill amends the Active Mobility Act 2017 to implement the new rules on PMAs to ensure their safe and responsible use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Second, the Bill amends the Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Act 2020 to make it an offence to keep an unsafe active mobility device (AMD).

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This grants LTA greater enforcement powers against devices that pose fire safety risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Since the landmark Active Mobility Act came into force in 2017, we have adjusted our laws multiple times to keep pace with a landscape that moves fast.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We introduced the Small Motorised Vehicles (Safety) Act 2020 to stem the flow of non-compliant devices into Singapore and the Shared Mobility Enterprises (Control and Licensing) Act 2020 to bring order to the business of shared AMDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Throughout this journey, we have witnessed a relentless desire for mobility options that are faster, cheaper and more convenient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: But ever so often, this came at the direct expense of path safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Following the ban on e-scooters from footpaths in 2019, we have seen a shift in misuse towards PMAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Regrettably, as soon as one regulatory gap is closed, another is exploited.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This underscores the need for this House to adjust our laws, not out of a desire to restrict and burden individuals with red tape, but out of a duty to curb misuse and keep our paths safe for all.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Many of us have heard from residents who feel increasingly unsafe as larger, faster devices weave through our paths under the guise of being mobility aids.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We need to restore the original purpose of these devices to serve their intended users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To recap, there are three main types of PMAs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: First, a mobility scooter, which is a motorised device with a single seat, steered with a handlebar and typically supported by a stem at the front of the device; two, a motorised wheelchair, which is propelled by a motor that forms part of the wheelchair and usually operated by a joystick; or three, a non-motorised wheelchair, which has no motor and is usually mounted on two or more wheels.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In this Bill, the first two, mobility scooters and motorised wheelchairs, will be regulated as "mobility vehicles".

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: As our population ages and more people have to use PMAs, there is a growing need to ensure that they are used safely and responsibly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We face a concerning trend of able-bodied individuals who are misusing mobility scooters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Although the device is a replacement for walking, some ride at top speeds on paths or operate large devices that endanger other path users, especially seniors and young children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Members, disability groups and the public have consistently called for the tightening of rules on PMAs and improvement in path safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This Bill thus takes a holistic approach to the problem of PMA misuse, speeding and oversized devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I will not specify the exact clauses as they span across the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Second, we will introduce dimension and weight limits for PMAs used on public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Fourth, we will also go upstream and require that mobility scooters are checked for compliance and registered before they are sold.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This upstream rule reduces the likelihood of users obtaining non-compliant mobility scooters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: All four measures were developed following discussions with the Active Mobility Advisory Panel (AMAP) and careful study of the issue and engagement with key user groups, including PMA users, disability groups, occupational therapists, general path users and food delivery riders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Since we announced the tightening of PMA rules in 2024, we have been working with stakeholders and user groups to prepare for the shift.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This includes readying the healthcare sector to conduct the assessment to grant a Certificate of Medical Need, also known as the Assessment for Mobility Scooter (AMS).

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have also been encouraging retailers to shift to new stocks of PMAs that are compliant with the new rules.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: First, we are reducing the speed limit for mobility scooters and motorised wheelchairs, also known as mobility vehicles, from 10 kilometres per hour to six kilometres per hour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Today, mobility vehicles have a 10-kilometre per hour limit, even if they travel on shared paths where the path speed limit is 25 kilometres per hour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This was recommended by the AMAP in 2018 and intended to discourage able-bodied misuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, experience has shown this limit to be insufficient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Mobility vehicles are generally larger and heavier than bicycles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Travelling at 10 kilometres per hour may still pose a danger to other path users, as it is much faster than typical walking speed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Displaying and advertising such non-compliant devices will carry penalties of up to $10,000 or imprisonment up to 12 months, or both.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To ease the transition, we will allow existing mobility vehicles with a device speed limit of up to 10 kilometres per hour to be used on public paths until 31 December 2028, but they need to ride within the six kilometres per hour limit and meet all other rules.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: From 1 January 2029 onwards, all mobility vehicles used on public paths must have a device speed limit of six kilometres per hour and below.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Second, we will introduce device dimension restrictions for PMAs to address the problem of large PMAs that inconvenience and endanger other path users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This will be aligned with the existing dimension restrictions on public transport.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Offenders caught riding such devices on public paths face penalties of up to $10,000 in fines or imprisonment of up to six months, or both, with penalties increasing for repea offences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Selling oversized mobility vehicles will be an offence, with penalties of up to $20,000 or imprisonment up to 24 months, or both, with higher penalties for non-individuals and repeat offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will require users to have a Certificate of Medical Need to ride a mobility scooter on public paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This targets the core problem of able-bodied users misusing devices meant for those with mobility needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: When we engaged stakeholders, they welcomed the recommendations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For example, some genuine users shared that the increased misuse of mobility scooters has caused them anxiety because they have had to deal with increasing scrutiny from the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Currently, we only intend to require certification for mobility scooters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We do not see a problem of misuse of motorised wheelchairs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: So, wheelchair users do not need a Certificate of Medical Need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The certificate will be available later this month, from 27 February 2026, through the AMS process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The assessment was developed jointly with the Ministry of Health (MOH), with input from professional healthcare associations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: A circular and guidelines were issued in November last year to prepare the sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Under the AMS, users with medical conditions which result in mobility difficulties will be certified to have a medical need to drive or ride a mobility scooter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Users can approach their regular doctor or occupational therapist for the assessment or a general practitioner who offers the service.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have worked with MOH to engage the healthcare sector to encourage clinics to offer the AMS so that it will be widely available.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Based on our survey of clinics, more than 140 clinics intend to offer the assessment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Users will have choices to help keep costs reasonable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Based on LTA's survey of clinics, fees are expected to range from $20 to $150, with a median fee of $50.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Given that a budget mobility scooter costs around $1,000 and mid-range models can reach up to $2,000, the cost of the assessment is relatively modest compared to the price of the device itself.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We hope users can understand that this would help to ensure that mobility scooters on public paths are only for those with genuine medical need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The charges will vary depending on the complexity of the consultation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have simplified the information that assessors have to provide to LTA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: They centre on three key things: first, whether the individual has a medical need to use a mobility scooter; second, whether this need is temporary or long term; and finally, whether the individual has a medical need for a device that exceeds the dimension requirements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: A list of clinics that offer the AMS will be available on LTA's website from tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Users should contact their preferred clinics directly to enquire about the cost and book an appointment in advance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We encourage users to consult their regular healthcare providers who already understand their medical history, to streamline the assessment process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We recognise that going to the doctor to obtain certification will take time and cost for users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will thus take a risk-managed approach to minimise the impact on our healthcare system and on genuine users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We recognise that as seniors age, the likelihood of mobility challenges increases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The risk of able-bodied seniors abusing mobility scooters is expected to be low.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This is especially given the reduced speed limit.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will monitor the situation and calibrate accordingly, if necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will also exempt users who have had their mobility needs or disability assessed and submitted relevant information to the Government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This includes existing beneficiaries of subsidised mobility scooters from the Seniors' Mobility and Enabling Fund (SMF) and Assistive Technology Fund (ATF).

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It also includes individuals already certified with Activities of Daily Living (ADL) needs in "mobility" or "transferring" who have applied for MOH disability schemes, such as the Home Caregiving Grant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These exemptions will apply automatically and users need not do anything.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Agencies will issue letters to notify existing SMF and ATF beneficiaries, as well as individuals with the relevant ADL needs who have applied for MOH disability schemes previously.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Moving forward, those applying to SMF for a subsidised mobility scooter will obtain the certificate as part of the subsidy application process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Those obtaining an ATF-subsidised mobility scooter and applicants for MOH disability schemes with the relevant ADL needs, will be automatically exempted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Going back to our intention of introducing this rule to curb misuse, our enforcement officers will focus on visibly able-bodied individuals misusing mobility scooters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Our intention is not to inconvenience genuine users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: So, I seek users' understanding that our enforcement officers will need to do their job and check for their certification at times.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It will also be an offence for businesses to employ or permit an individual to ride a mobility scooter on public path during the course of work, without ensuring that the rider has valid Certification of Medical Need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Offenders will face penalties of up to $2,000 in fines or imprisonment of up to six months, or both.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This is similar to how it is an offence for businesses employing or permitting an individual to ride a power-assisted bicycle (PAB) in the course of work, without ensuring the rider has the mandatory theory test certification.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Fourth, we will require mobility scooters to be registered with LTA to strengthen upstream enforcement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Today, PABs and e-scooters need to be registered with LTA to ensure devices comply with rules and are affixed with identification marks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To strengthen upstream enforcement and improve the overall effectiveness of PMA measures, mobility scooters will need to be registered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Only mobility scooters that comply with device dimension and speed restrictions can be registered to persons with valid Certificates of Medical Need, exempted persons or whitelisted businesses, such as retailers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: In addition, LTA and the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) will make clear through an industry circular that mobility scooters fall under the classification of medical devices as they are specifically designed for individuals with walking difficulties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This means that under HSA's regulations, importers must have an HSA licence and list their devices on HSA's database before import.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: LTA will only allow mobility scooter models that are listed on HSA's database of medical devices to be registered.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Existing mobility scooters need not meet this requirement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: To ensure the registration regime is effective, it must apply to all mobility scooters eventually.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: If we exempt existing mobility scooters, it will be challenging to distinguish new devices from existing ones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The sale of an unregistered mobility scooter for use on public paths will be an offence from 1 June 2026, with individuals facing penalties of up to $20,000 or jail of up to 24 months, or both, and higher penalties for non-individuals and repeat offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Offenders face penalties of up to $2,000 or jail of up to three months, or both, with higher penalties for repeat offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We have designed the registration process to minimise burden on users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For devices sold from 1 June 2026, retailers will handle registration, creating a seamless experience for consumers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For existing devices, we will give some time for users to register their devices ahead of the requirement by 1 January 2029.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Users will be able to register their devices, if they are compliant, at roving stations that LTA will roll out in mid-2027 at community touchpoints.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Devices registered as part of this exercise need not be listed on HSA's database of medical devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I know many users may want to rush to register their devices ahead of the rules.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: LTA will include a survey link on its website for users to indicate their interest in registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This will help us to better deploy resources for the roving registration stations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I must emphasise here that only compliant mobility scooters will be allowed for registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: If you have a mobility scooter that does not comply with the six kilometres per hour device speed limit or dimension and weight limits, please replace your device.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These new rules were announced two years ago in March 2024 and users should transition to compliant devices by 1 January 2029 – almost five years later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: LTA has engaged retailers on the new registration requirements and we will provide guidance to roll this out smoothly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For AMD retailers, many will be familiar with the existing registration regimes for power-assisted bicycles and e-scooters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will pay special attention to medical device retailers who may be less familiar with the process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We want to ensure genuine users have access to PMAs, which can significantly improve their quality of life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: At the same time, we need to keep paths safe and address the problem of misuse.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We will also keep the registration process streamlined and user-friendly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Thus far, we have focused on the PMA proposals, which are intended to strengthen path safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Turning to fire safety, the Government takes a strict enforcement approach towards the import, sale and use of non-compliant AMDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Since 2021, local retailers must seek LTA's approval for the import of PABs and PMDs, and they must be registered before use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: These devices must also be compliant with safety standards.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: For PABs, it is the EN15194 standard, while for registrable PMDs, it is the UL2272 standard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Despite years of regulatory tightening since 2016, we continue to grapple with the fire safety risks from AMDs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: PMDs accounted for most cases at 31, and the bulk of PMD fires involve non-UL2272-certified devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We can do more to prevent such fires and we will do more.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Today, it is an offence to ride a non-UL2272-certified e-scooter on public paths or roads, but not to keep such devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This means that if LTA enforcement officers come across a non-UL2272-certified e-scooter, no action can be taken unless it is being used.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: This is unlike the case for non-compliant power-assisted bicycles, where it is already an offence to keep such a device under the Road Traffic Act 1961.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Devices that do not comply with the prescribed safety requirements, such as the UL2272 safety standard for registrable personal mobility devices, will be unsafe devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Some may ask why we are only doing this now.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: LTA's mandate has traditionally focused on path and road safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: However, recognising the fire safety risks of AMDs even when they are not used on paths or roads, we are extending the function and duty of the LTA to include the regulation of the keeping of unsafe devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Clause 46 will amend the Land Transport Authority of Singapore Act 1995 to expand LTA's function and duty to include regulating the keeping of unsafe devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: The Bill will make it an offence to keep such unsafe devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: LTA will leverage feedback received via official channels and social media, surveillance as well as day-to-day operations to detect and seize non-UL2272 e-scooters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: It will enable those with mobility needs who genuinely need to use PMAs to use them safely alongside other path users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Ultimately, Mr Speaker, we must return to the heart of this matter: the vision of a gracious "we first" society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: MOT and LTA are strengthening our laws and enforcement, but they are not a panacea.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: We must acknowledge the reality that the "cat" – the regulator – will never be fast enough to catch every "mouse" – every errant rider.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Path safety is and must always be a collective responsibility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Errant riders and device owners must realise that they are not just breaking the law but endangering themselves and our communities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: Responsible riders among us must also speak up and help shape the right culture on our paths.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: While the Government will do its part through regulations, infrastructure and enforcement, it is the individual's behaviour and the community's social norms that will ultimately make our paths safe for everyone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Transport (Mr Baey Yam Keng)
text: I will now invite the Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs to address the MHA components of this joint Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, to strengthen the regulatory framework around speed limiters to better deter and detect non-compliance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, to clarify that the mandatory disqualification periods prescribed for certain offences under the Road Traffic Act are minimum periods and that the Courts can impose longer disqualification periods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I will focus my remarks on these two amendments, before briefly touching on the other amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Members will recall that in 2024, we commenced the mandatory installation of speed limiters in lorries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is to mitigate the risks posed by heavy vehicles, which can cause more severe consequences in the event of an accident.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have adopted a phased implementation approach, depending on the weight and registration date of the vehicle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have reviewed the existing speed limiter offences and found them to be inadequate in deterring non-compliance and there are also gaps in accountability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: To close these gaps, clause 56 of the Bill introduces several new offences and raises the penalties for existing offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: First, we will hold owners and drivers liable for knowingly causing or permitting the use of non-compliant speed limiter-required lorries and for tampering with installed speed limiters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Under the current speed limiter rules, only the driver commits an offence for driving a non-compliant lorry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, there may be situations where such non-compliance occurs under the instruction of the owner of the lorry, who is not liable under the existing rules.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The proposed amendment closes this gap by extending the scope of the offence to anyone who knowingly causes or permits the use of a non-compliant lorry, including the owner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In addition, while tampering with a speed limiter is already an offence, currently, only the person who tampered with it is liable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The current law does not expressly make liable, persons who instructed or caused another person to do so, nor persons who offer to alter speed limiters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our proposed amendment ensures that all parties who are involved in speed limiter tampering can be held accountable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, we will impose a duty on Authorised Agents to report suspected tampering of a speed limiter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Currently, only Authorised Agents of the Traffic Police may install or service speed limiters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: With this amendment, such agents will be required to notify the Traffic Police if they know or have reason to believe that a speed limiter has been tampered with or is non-compliant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This will enable prompt investigation and removal of non-compliant lorries from the roads.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Third, we will prohibit the advertising of speed limiter services by unauthorised parties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This deters the supply of illegal tampering services and reduces opportunities for tampering.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Bill will also raise the penalties for existing speed limiter-related offences.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Currently, first-time offenders face a fine of up to $1,000 or imprisonment of up to three months, while repeat offenders face a fine of up to $2,000 or imprisonment of up to six months.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These penalties have not been updated since 1999.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This ensures that the penalties are a credible deterrent and are commensurate with the potential harm posed by speeding heavy vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The disqualification period that the Court may impose can be any period equal to or above the prescribed minimum disqualification period, including a lifetime disqualification period if it thinks fit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These amendments seek to address the observations in the recent High Court judgment of Ng En You Jeremiah v Public Prosecutor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The High Court, in considering a sentencing framework for the relevant driving offence, noted that the offence already imposed a mandatory 12-year disqualification period, “unless the court for special reasons thinks fit to not order or to order otherwise”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The High Court also held that “special reasons” had to be exceptional and that the 12-year disqualification period should apply regardless of the applicable sentencing band for that particular driving offence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The High Court's judgment thus appears to suggest that special reasons must be present before a Court may impose a disqualification period that is longer than the prescribed minimum period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For serious road traffic offences, such as driving under the influence of drink and car racing, a mandatory minimum disqualification period is prescribed because such conduct poses a serious risk to public safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Clauses 68, 74 and 79 will enhance the operational efficiency of the Singapore Armed Forces and Traffic Police.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Clause 68 addresses an ambiguity under section 49 of the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Currently, the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) contracts commercial bus companies to ferry soldiers to various locations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In view of the shortage of bus drivers, SAF intends for its personnel to drive the commercial buses it leases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, section 49 may be interpreted to limit SAF personnel holding military driving licences to driving only vehicles owned by SAF.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Currently, Police officers are required to manually review, themselves, images and footages captured by Police cameras and manually issue, themselves, the traffic notices, even for straightforward violations, such as red-light beating and speeding.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Clause 82 amends section 4 of the Road Vehicles (Special Powers) Act relating to the forfeiture of road vehicles used to commit any offence prescribed in the Schedule of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Forfeiture is currently mandatory if the Court is satisfied that a road vehicle has been used to commit any scheduled offence or to convey persons to the scene or facilitate escape of any person from the scene where a scheduled offence has been committed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: MHA remains concerned by the road safety situation and has plans to further tighten our laws and regulatory framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will share more at the upcoming Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We also call upon all road users to exercise responsibility, patience and graciousness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is possible to achieve zero road injuries and fatalities but only if we all do our part.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Today’s debate on the Land Transport and Related Matters Bill reflects this and is therefore of public importance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Our Transport Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) is giving this Bill close attention, as are many of our People’s Action Party (PAP) Parliamentary colleagues.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A total of 18 PAP Members of Parliament (MPs) will speak on the new regulations on PMAs, ERP 2.0, vehicle safety and other related issues.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In the course of our respective work on the ground, my PAP colleagues and I have engaged different stakeholder groups, including private hire drivers, union workers, industry representatives and, of course, our own residents.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: These engagements gave us precious opportunities to hear their feedback first-hand, understand their lived experiences and challenges faced and gather practical suggestions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: My PAP colleagues will share more in their speeches.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: At the heart of our interest is the principle of ensuring fair, inclusive and safe use of our public roads and space.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: In a society where our people have diverse needs, co-existence is key.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: This means that our public infrastructure and spaces offer choices and accommodate different user groups, and that our legislations enable people yet protect the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Overall, my fellow PAP MPs and I support the intent of the Bill and we will set out our arguments in our respective speeches.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We will also be highlighting our concerns pertaining to practical implementation, costs and impact on vulnerable groups, such as low-income groups and platform workers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Here, allow me to raise a few points.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Real-time data collected via the OBUs can be integrated with existing systems to enable situational awareness and faster incident detection.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Over time, these data can support incident and demand predictions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Removing physical ERP gantries eventually will also free up valuable land space.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Second, OBUs are central to ERP 2.0, but the installation was delayed by the global chip shortage from 2021 to 2023.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Even longer, if you consider that the OBUs were based on the technology back in 2013.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Given how rapidly technology evolves, how will the Government ensure that the hardware and software, including the operating system, do not become obsolete before we can achieve the smart transport management objectives?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Upgrading devices is costly in manpower and money, and it places burdens on vehicle owners.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: So, we really do not want a situation whereby very shortly after we complete the OBU deployment in 2027, and then we have to go into another round again.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Third, the use of OBUs will make distance-based ERP pricing feasible.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I understand the Minister mentioned that it will not be an immediate deployment, but it is feasible.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: These workers will be unable to optimise pathways and can only be “price takers” in this instance.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: So, in the eventual situation whereby distance-based ERP pricing is implemented, may I ask what measures will be in place to support these workers?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Fourth, PMAs are increasingly important, particularly in an ageing society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Many elderly residents depend on them for mobility and well-being.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But irresponsible use poses real safety risks to both the device users and others around them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Today, there are effectively no restrictions on who may use mobility scooters.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I have personally seen riders moving at high speeds on pedestrian paths and instances of multiple able-bodied users on a single scooter endangering others.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Just to illustrate with an example from a few years ago, I witnessed three young and able-bodied persons riding a mobility scooter along the covered walkway cutting through Circuit Road.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I stopped the scooter and attempted to tell the three riders to dismount as it was dangerous.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: They gave me a puzzled look and then sped off.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Unfortunately, I did not manage to chase them down.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: That was perhaps the most outrageous instance I encountered and thankfully, the only time so far.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Next, strong enforcement is critical to achieving the Bill’s objectives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Officers cannot be everywhere; active mobility patrols rely heavily on volunteers and camera deployments have been piecemeal and temporary.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: And when they are removed, problems often recur.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: For example, after temporary cameras were installed in 2024 on the pedestrian bridge between Paya Lebar Way and Aljunied Crescent in MacPherson, compliance improved.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But the problem of riders speeding cross the bridge returned once the cameras were taken down.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: As such, how will the Government strengthen enforcement capacity?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Will more permanent cameras be installed and can our network of cameras support intelligent, real-time monitoring to identify and act, whether it is through warnings or issuance of notices, on non-compliant PMA riders more promptly?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I should add that this should include wilful cyclists and other mobility device users as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Keeping such a device tempts one to still use it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Moreover, if it cannot be used, then there is no reason to keep it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A key shift in this Bill is the reclassification of what we currently know as PMAs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Bill replaces this term with a new legal category: "mobility vehicles".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This category, in part, encompasses both motorised wheelchairs and mobility scooters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I will first speak briefly on ERP 2.0, while the rest of my speech will focus on the regime changes for these mobility vehicles and raising several concerns.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This marks the departure from the privacy-centric design of ERP 1.0.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As noted in The Straits Times article on 16 April 1993, the registry of vehicles explicitly chose a system using prepaid smart card so that, I quote: "all the information is in the card and not with the authorities managing the system".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the old IU kept trip data local, the new OBUs enable continuous central logging.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Minister clarify what specific technical encryption and anonymisation protocols are applied to data transmitted from the OBU to the central server?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, what are the legal safeguards to prevent this data from being accessed by other agencies for purposes entirely unrelated to road pricing?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This includes bicycles, PABs, PMDs and of course, PMAs or mobility vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Yet on a daily basis we still witness widespread disregard for road safety, cyclists and PAB users not keeping left, beating red lights, riding without helmets or using footpaths with little regard for pedestrians.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is notwithstanding statistics revealed by the Traffic Police, I think it was yesterday, of 650 summons issued to errant cyclists in the first half of 2025.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How many cyclists or e-bike riders are aware, for example, that it is an offence riding on the right side of a motor vehicle unless they are overtaking or about to make a right turn?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is also not uncommon to see riders not riding on the left lanes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Are users of rental bikes made aware that helmets must be worn when riding on the roads?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In December, a 71-year-old lady was severely injured by an e-bike while exiting Pasir Ris Mall, requiring jaw reconstruction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In January, another lady in her 60s suffered torn ligaments and fractures after being knocked down while crossing the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In November last year, the Minister of State, Baey Yam Keng himself, was bumped into by a female cyclist travelling in the wrong direction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such in these incidents underscore a poor riding culture rooted in years of inadequate public education and enforcement, points I raised repeatedly in this House since 2017.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am reminded of the Road Safety Park at East Coast launched in the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Its objective was ambitious then: to introduce road safety as a way of life.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: By its 20th year, more than one million students in Singapore had passed through its gates to participate in traffic games.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They role played as pedestrians and drivers to internalise road courtesy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This was a society wide effort that instil safety consciousness through practical engagement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To truly change our AMD riding culture, we must move beyond static signage to immersive learning.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The road safety park's success in the early years shows that when we have the will to invest, we can shape an entire generation's behaviour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Authorities have cited limited resources as far as AMDs are concerned.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Recently, Minister of State Baey Yam Keng reiterated that LTA will do its best within constraints.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But Mr Speaker, there should be a greater political will to invest in the resources needed for a safer riding culture and for safer footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While these measures directly address concerns regarding the misuse of mobility scooters by able bodied individuals, speeding and the use of oversized devices, I am again concerned about the practical execution of the measures designed in this Bill, given the inability to significantly improve safe use and riding culture for different forms of AMDs so far.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will LTA ensure non-compliant mobility scooters are not used after 2028, or unauthorised riders do not continue with their use after the passing of this Bill?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The same gap worries me about clause 84 to 91, regarding the proposed banning of non UL2272 e-scooters or PMDs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is disturbing that five years after PMDs or e-scooters were supposedly banned from mainstream use, except on park connectors, they are still the main cause of fires for all AMDs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One can imagine how many more are kept in homes and continue to be used.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is also reflective, at least to some extent, of the effectiveness of past and former enforcement efforts in curbing non-compliant use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On 20 November 2025, an island-wide operation targeted non-compliant devices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What measures were taken for units where occupants were not at home?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Five years after the ban, they remain a primary fire risk.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will the offence of keeping these PMDs be enforced on a regular basis?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Could the Ministry consider concentrating officers in a specific zone for a sustained period for intensive enforcement?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This will send a strategic message rather than spreading our limited resources too thinly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The reduction of mobility scooter speed limit to six kilometres per hour raises some concerns, and I have spoken on this in this House previously.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Minister clarify whether any studies were conducted on the impact of this reduction on the travel range of elderly users?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some of my residents who use their PMAs to travel beyond their immediate neighbourhood had provided feedback to me that the reduction in speed will increase the time they need to travel and ultimately, reduce the distance they can travel within the time that they have.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Mobility scooters do provide seniors with confidence to be out and about, which is a good thing.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, for these individuals, mobility scooters can be invaluable at maintaining mobility, independence and quality of life during their golden years, allowing broader access to seniors above 70 would empower them to remain active and engaged in community life, promoting both physical and mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I would also like to suggest that the Government could explore expanding the capacity of occupational therapies in restructured hospitals to provide mobility scooters, assessments and training.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This would ensure that seniors and others with genuine mobility needs receive proper guidance on the safe and responsible use of these devices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such a measure would not only enhance user safety but also foster greater confidence among the public in the appropriate use of mobility scooters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, outreach to existing users who have to discontinue use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am also concerned about the impact on existing mobility scooter users who have to discontinue their existing use of mobility scooters.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: There are some parents who use their mobility scooters to ferry their young children or some seniors who ferry their spouses with mobility or health issues on their existing PMAs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These PMAs will not be authorised under this Bill due to their sizes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must be sensitive to understand that some of these individuals have real transportation needs that in their views are not adequately met by the proposals in this Bill or what is otherwise available out there.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, how will LTA reach out to these affected individuals effectively on the law change and get them to understand the risks perceived by the authorities as posed by such devices on the users and fellow footpath users, and to get their buy-in on the new law?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The law disallows PMAs from riding on the roads, presumably except when crossing roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In 2019 and 2020, I raised in this House how narrow or blocked footpaths in, for example, private estates, would usually force PMA riders onto roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In January 2023, I had asked in a Parliamentary Question about statistics of enforcement against PMA riders who were caught on the road and the range of punishments imposed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am surprised by the low statistics of enforcement cited.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I agree that it may not be safe for PMAs to use the road, I recognise that our infrastructure needs to catch up to ensure that there is no reason for PMA riders to use the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Today, in 2026, we are slowing these seniors down even further to six kilometres per hour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If we are going to enforce a strict walking pace and a strict road ban, the Government must first guarantee that the last mile footpath in our private estates, for example, are actually wide enough and clear enough to be used.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, are the pavements free of obstacles and trees to allow free access?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Otherwise, it is unfair and unsafe for elderly PMA users.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If our seniors are forced to use the road, they should not fear being prosecuted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the other hand, from my conversation with many mobility scooter riders, it seems that many are still not even aware that it is illegal to use their mobility scooters on the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This brings us to the same familiar problem of the need for more and better public education and adequate regular enforcement, as is the case for other AMDs, which I touched on earlier.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In closing, Mr Speaker, I hope the Government will consider the proposals and suggestions I have made.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Notwithstanding my concerns and reservations, I support the Bill's intent to improve safety and better regulation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I urge the Ministry to ensure strong public education, effective enforcement and thoughtful implementation so that we build a safer environment for all.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These are important objectives and I support them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: But as we consider these changes, we must remain clear-eyed about who will be most affected on the ground, especially our workers, many of whom depend on our transport system not just to get around, but to earn a living.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I declare my interests as Assistant Secretary-General of the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), Advisor to the National Delivery Champions Association (NDCA) and Executive Secretary to the National Transport Workers' Union.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These measures are meant to improve safety for all footpath users and that is a goal we all share.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We must be careful not to unintentionally place additional hardship on persons with genuine, often permanent mobility impairments, many of whom rely on PMAs to undertake delivery work as their primary and sometimes, only source of income.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: For our riders, platform work is not a convenience.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: It is a hard-won pathway to financial independence.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: First, the reduction in PMA speed limits will lengthen delivery times.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: For riders who are already push themselves daily, those extra minutes compound quickly.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Fewer completed jobs mean lower earnings, and for riders living close to the edge, even a modest drop in income can translate into real trade-offs between food, utilities or even medical needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Media reports have already highlighted concerns that riders' earnings may be significantly affected and these reflect what we are hearing consistently on the ground through our union engagements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: She fully supports the intent behind these safety measures, especially to protect young children who may be too small to be seen easily by riders and are particularly vulnerable to careless riding.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: At the same time, Hana is also a full-time delivery rider who relies on her PMA for her work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This illustrates the real tension we must address between improving safety and ensuring that riders who depend on this work are not pushed into financial hardship.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I also urge the Government to work closely with platform operators to monitor post-implementation impacts and to be prepared to offer targeted transitional support if hardship emerges.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Second, while I support the Certificate of Medical Need to prevent abuse, the criteria must not be so rigid that deserving users are excluded.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: We should avoid overly narrow thresholds that unintentionally create new barriers for those who genuinely need PMAs for safe and independent mobility.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In our engagements with our PMA riders, we see a wide range of profiles and needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Some, like Ms Toh Bee Tin – a familiar name to many in this House as she was a Para Table Tennis athlete – are born with mobility disabilities and rely entirely on their PMAs, not just for mobility, but for their delivery livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Others, like Ms Siti Sabarinah, turned to a PMA after suffering a serious leg injury from a delivery cycling accident last year.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: While she is on the path to recovery, she is still unable to walk independently over longer distances.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: For riders like her, the concern is not just access today, but the longevity and viability of a significant PMA investment under the new regulatory framework.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These examples remind us that eligibility should be guided by real functional needs, not narrow thresholds.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: As we tighten safeguards against misuse, we must also ensure that those who genuinely depend on PMAs for safe, independent mobility and to earn a living are not left behind.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This includes expenses, such as medical certifications and installations of attached-on speedometers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In addition, NDCA is in discussion with affiliate general practitioner (GP) partners to make medical assessments and certification more affordable and accessible.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These efforts reflect our shared commitment to upholding road safety, while also protecting the dignity and sustainability of work for those who rely on PMAs to earn an honest living.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I also ask the Government to consider additional support measures, especially for riders, like Siti, who are recovering from health conditions and will eventually need to transition out of PMAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Support during this transition period is important, so that recovery does not come at the cost of livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: In addition, I seek the Government's consideration for assistance with the purchase of essential equipment, such as speedometers, which will be critical in helping riders comply with this new speed limit.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Third, while I appreciate the advance notice given since 2024 and the meaningful consultations with NDCA, I urge an education-first approach during the initial enforcement.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Some users will need time to adapt, whether to speed limits, device requirements or certification rules.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Reasonable grace periods and room for discretion, especially for genuine mistakes, will go a long way in ensuring compliance without undue stress.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Clear rules matter but compassionate implementation matters just as much.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: The NDCA has engaged riders extensively across Singapore not just in meeting rooms, but where our riders actually work and rest.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: These sessions covered recruitment, rider safety, enforcement issues, Central Provident Fund (CPF) clarifications, last-mile delivery challenges and discussions with LTA and our platform operators.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I support the amendments to section 6 of the LTA of Singapore Act 1995 recognising the promotion and regulation for the safe use of electric vehicles (EVs).

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This is no small matter and whether we can navigate this path steadily depends mostly on our bus captains.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Currently, companies do provide training, but each has different arrangements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: When manpower is tight, training is sometimes shortened.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They drive large vehicles with complex systems, carrying passengers and bear heavy responsibility.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Some captains have told us that driving electric buses requires not only getting used to new equipment and rules, but also constantly monitoring screens, unlike before when it is mostly monitoring through the rear mirrors.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Over time, this causes eye strain and even dizziness.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Road safety must always remain our top priority.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: Measures that protect lives on our roads are necessary and I recognise fully the intent behind mandating speed limiters for heavy vehicles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This intent is also understood and broadly supported by the fleet operators and lorry owners whom I have spoken with.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: That said, as with many transport policies, the real test lies not in the intent, but actually, in the implementation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: One key concern raised by drivers and operators relates to speed differentials on our expressways.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This wide gap can disrupt traffic flow, lead to frequent overtaking, sudden braking and in some cases, paradoxically increasing accident risks rather than reduce them.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: This creates uneven road behaviour and undermines both safety objectives as well as fair competition.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: They must be complemented by consistent enforcement, clear lane discipline and policies that reflect the realities of mixed traffic conditions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Punggol)
text: I, therefore, urge the relevant Ministries to continue engaging drivers and operators to apply enforcement with judgement, and to ensure that implementation remains practical, fair and grounded in real-world conditions so that our roads are not just regulated, but genuinely safer for everyone.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: At the outset, let me state that I recognise the importance of ensuring safety and order for all users in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Our roads, footpaths and shared spaces must be safe for pedestrians, cyclists, persons with disabilities and motorists.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As mobility patterns and technologies evolve, our laws must be updated to reflect these new realities on the ground.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: One of the most significant developments in recent years has been the rapid rise in the use of mobility devices, such as PMAs, PMDs and PABs.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Their use is not limited to elderly Singaporeans or persons with visible disabilities.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Even working adults, caregivers and delivery workers are using them, which reflects the last mile connectivity challenges they face.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The increased use of mobility vehicles by Singaporeans is more often than not driven by a practical need.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans rely on this informal low-cost mobility solution simply to get by and get on with their daily lives.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: With the Certificate of Entitlement prices shattering records year after year, a private car is now firmly out of reach for many working families.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Even motorcycles, traditionally seen as an affordable alternative, have become significantly more expensive.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Against this backdrop, it should come as no surprise that to meet their everyday transport needs, Singaporeans have turned to mobility vehicles that cost from a few hundred dollars, to $1,000 or $2,000 – just a fraction of the price of a motorcycle or a car.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For many Singaporeans, these devices are the only viable way to bridge the last mile between their homes and essential destinations, such as workplaces, schools, markets and food centres.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: There have been genuine incidents involving reckless riding, excessive speeds and conflicts on footpaths.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These issues must be addressed, but we must be careful not to inadvertently cause hardship to Singaporeans who rely on these devices out of necessity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Many such individuals now use mobility vehicles to earn a living, including completing food and parcel deliveries for platform companies, such as Grab.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For them, these vehicles are essential tools of work rather than toys for amusement or recreation.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While some workers will be able to make up for this by working longer hours, others who have caregiving needs or health problems may not be able to do so.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Besides being a tool for employment, mobility vehicles can also prove to be the most convenient or practical option for some residents to get around the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Take a resident who lives at Block 530 in Bedok North Street 3, which is right next to Kaki Bukit Community Centre.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: To head to Red Swastika School, the resident has no direct bus route.
