speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: There are indirect bus options, but this involves switching either at Bedok Interchange or at Heartbeat at Bedok.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And that will take more than 35 minutes.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The other option is to walk 1.2 kilometres, which Google Maps indicate will take around 17 minutes.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: To reach Bedok Reservoir Park or Damai Secondary School, the resident has two options to walk – 1.9 kilometres for 26 minutes or to walk one kilometre for 14 minutes to a bus stop near along Bedok North Avenue 3; and then take a three-minute bus ride for three stops.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Rather, they are meant to demonstrate that for certain short but significant journeys in Kaki Bukit, there are sometimes no direct or convenient public transport options.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The only realistic alternative is to walk directly from point to point.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is the healthiest option, but may be challenging for the elderly, those with mobility difficulties or parents with young children who are pressed for time – not to mention the hot and humid weather in Singapore, which does not make for a comfortable walking experience.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In such circumstances, a PMA can be useful, especially for caregivers with children or working workers rushing to and from shifts.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Transport policy should be concerned with more than efficiency and safety, but also consider equity and inclusion, especially for those with the least resources.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As I mentioned earlier, the increasing reliance on AMDs is driven by practical necessity.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Residents turn to these devices to cope with and adapt to what they see as gaps in our public transport network, especially when it comes to last mile connectivity or travelling to neighbourhood amenities that are just slightly too far to walk to comfortably.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For such persons, mobility devices are the most viable options, after taking cost, time, convenience and accessibility into account.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As such, improving our public transport links, including boosting capacity for last mile connectivity must be a priority.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We can even call this the "we first" shuttle.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These local shuttles should be targeted to the specific practical needs of residents and reflect how they actually get around the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This may reduce their reliance on mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These improvements would also make our public transport network more fit for purpose for our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Our elderly should find it easy and convenient to take a bus for a few stops to visit their friends or run errands in another part of the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The service is intended to provide coverage for "short but significant" journeys around the neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Public transport is still limited for short journeys like these.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The proposed community buses should target the specific practical needs of residents and reflect how they get around their neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This can help to reduce reliance on mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: These measures can align our public transport network with the needs of senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: They should view taking bus rides as something very convenient.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: They should not have to choose between walking or using mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And I think we are responsible for providing bus journeys free of charge to senior citizens.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Over there, they call it the "Freedom Pass".

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We should provide a similar service for our senior citizens and give them a "Merdeka Pass" to travel freely on our public transport. : Mr Speaker, this Bill is an opportunity to consider how different modes of mobility may necessitate the long-term transformation of our last mile connectivity infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The mobility devices that we are discussing today are here to stay.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, if pedestrian safety is our concern, this is best achieved by segregating pedestrian traffic from motor-powered mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We can achieve this by moving more decisively towards a more coherent and integrated network of dedicated cycling paths that are clearly separated from pedestrian footpaths, wherever possible and then confining the use of mobility devices to these cycling paths.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Currently, this is not possible in many neighbourhoods where cycling paths share space with pedestrian footpaths.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It requires us to fundamentally rethink how we allocate existing road space, rather than incrementally increasing cycling and non-pedestrian infrastructure at the margins.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In this way, we also make space for the safe use of mobility devices.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We must address the structural gaps that drive people to rely on mobility devices in the first place.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This means investing in better neighbourhood connectivity, more responsive public transport planning and infrastructure that reflects and facilitates how people actually move around their communities.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Over the past few years, misuse of PMAs have resulted in nuisance to pedestrians, injuries and even deaths to PMA users.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They have also caused severe negative externalities including fires that result in property damage and loss of lives.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is finally time to reset the original intent of PMAs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Bill's amendments are well-thought out and eliminate most scenarios of misuse, while preserving as much inclusivity as possible for genuine users.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Notwithstanding, I would like to raise a few concerns.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They are also worried that they are unable to get a doctor's letter.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: To be clear, I agree that the inclusion of all seniors above age 70 is an efficient way to implement the policy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: What I am worried about is over-exclusion of a specific group; that is, a small group that needs PMAs but may now be excluded.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Some of them may even have been using PMAs to earn a livelihood, such as food delivery.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: And given their physical limitations, it may not be possible for them to switch to using other transport modes like PABs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Also, for those in their 50s and 60s, they may not be able to secure other forms of employment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I do recognise that this is indeed a difficult provision to make in terms of legislation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I agree that the inclusion of all senior citizens aged 70 and above is an efficient way to implement the policy, but my concern is the possibility of over-exclusion of a specific group.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There is a small group of individuals who require PMAs but may no longer be eligible.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Some of them also use PMAs to earn a living, such as food delivery.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Given their physical limitations, it may be difficult for them to switch to other modes of transport such as PABs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Furthermore, for those in their 50s and 60s, they may face difficulties securing other forms of employment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Although this group is small, I hope that LTA will consider extending conditional PMA user eligibility to them, provided they have no record of prior speeding offences.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I do recognise that such provisions are indeed difficult to implement from a legal standpoint. : Sembawang West constituency happens to have quite a lot of PMAs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Many of them are plying on shared paths with pedestrians.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Several residents, especially the more elderly pedestrians, have given feedback that some PMA users are rude and dominate the shared paths, sometimes, in a dangerous way while others blast loud music even late at night.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: These bad behaviours cause near-accidents, especially when pedestrians are forced to make way for them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They also cause noise pollution as the loud music reverberates, sometimes, jolting residents resting at home from their sleep.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: However, the new rules in the Bill's amendments do not address these behaviours and I am concerned that such eligible but errant PMA users may continue to behave like they own the shared paths.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Again, I recognise that it is difficult to use laws to constrain such behaviour, as eligibility criteria should be based on objective need, not social behavioural norms.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Yet, the latter are the stuff of our everyday experience in our homes and towns, and they make a big difference between the safe, quiet enjoyment of our space, or an experience of risk, danger and high emotions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: (In Mandarin):   Within the Sembawang West constituency, the use of PMAs is quite prevalent, with a considerable portion operating on paths shared with pedestrians.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I have received feedback from many residents, particularly the elderly, regarding some PMA users who are rude on shared paths and dominate lanes inappropriately, sometimes, in a dangerous way.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There are also users who blast loud music late at night.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: These behaviours cause dangerous situations when pedestrians are forced to give way, whilst also generating noise in residential areas that affects residents' rest at home.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Although these issues are isolated incidents, their impact on the community's safety and quality of life cannot be overlooked.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: However, the current amendments focus primarily on usage eligibility and technical specifications, and do not directly address behavioural issues.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I am concerned that some PMA users who meet the eligibility criteria but engage in inappropriate behaviour may continue to use their device improperly on shared paths.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: I understand that it is not easy to regulate such social behaviours through legal means.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Eligibility for PMA usage should be based on objective need rather than subjective behavioural assessments.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Nevertheless, these behaviours represent real situations that residents face in daily life and directly affect the peace and safety of common spaces.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Beyond defining usage eligibility, I would like to ask the Minister whether LTA could consider complementary measures, such as establishing courses or workshops for PMA users to guide them in responsible usage of PMAs, enhance safety awareness and thereby, better safeguard the safety of both pedestrians and users. : Another concern is related to implementation challenges.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Although PMAs are currently not required to be registered with LTA and hence, we do not know how many PMAs there are nation-wide.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The success of this new rule is highly dependent on the speed and comprehensiveness of enforcement operations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Enforcement officers are usually stationed at designated locations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The ineligible users will be on alert and will avoid these officers who can be seen from far, even though they may be wearing plain clothes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Some users may be still riding their PMAs late at night, which are hard to see from far.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The second enforcement process is related to oversized PMAs and non-UL2722 compliant e-scooters.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Over the past years, I have received many residents' feedback on their neighbours parking or even charging their oversized PMAs or non-UL2722 compliant e-scooters along HDB flats' common corridors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They are not only a source of fire hazard.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They can also become obstructions during emergency escape.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Wearing my Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment GPC hat, I hope LTA will set up collection points for these vehicles to be deposited and thereafter, arrange for them to be sold and be used in overseas markets.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Alternatively, I urge LTA to arrange for these disposed PMAs and e-scooters to be scrapped and parts be recycled appropriately so that they do not create a new problem for our environment.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There will be more seniors who will need PMAs to move around.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Let us reset the original intent of PMAs as a mobility aid.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Let us protect and support our seniors and those with mobility challenges.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Let us put a stop to unnecessary injuries and deaths due to PMA and PMD fires.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Let us keep our homes safe for everyone.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I support the core objectives and the amendments being tabled before us today but would like to seek clarifications relating to how the enforcement of the new regime to regulate the use of PMAs will take place and in particular, how these policies are developed in conjunction with the AMAP.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One of the key questions that I have relates to how authorities propose the enforcement take place against PMA users who are potentially breaching the upcoming rules.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the amendments introduce the Certificate of Medical Need system, how would trying to catch users without the requisite certification look like in practice?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, would enforcement officers be required to identify potential rule breakers based on clear rationale?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For instance, whether the certificate or the registration mark is visible on the mobility scooter?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While circumstances like having multiple people squeezing onto a mobility scooter might be a reasonable means of identification, as it is unlikely that multiple people travelling to the same location may have mobility affecting disabilities, I am concerned that casual, visual perception of able-bodiedness would be used instead.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How will enforcement officers thus identify these users and how will we ensure that certified PMA users just trying to move about their everyday lives are not subject to constant interruption or compliance checks?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having clear published guidelines will also help with public education efforts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is especially important given that we can see from various news reports that so many of the confrontations between PMA users and pedestrians take place without an enforcement officer present.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How can we ensure that vigilante justice will not rear its ugly head with passers-by leaping to hasty or even erroneous conclusions about whether or not a PMA user is indeed eligible?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having spoken to people with disabilities and advocacy groups, it remains common in our society to visually perceive able-bodiedness, including in the national press.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must avoid such stigma being perpetuated inadvertently.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In view of the concerns above, can the Government share how it proposes to address with them with a view to ensure that misconceptions about what disability means, visible or hidden, affecting young or old are not further entrenched?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Disabled People's Association highlighted this point in their comments on this Bill, stating that a one- to two-year implementation period would be more comparable to other laws, such as the Workplace Fairness Act.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With the new regulations adding quite a few requirements to the already extensive rules on active mobility, I believe it would be fair to give users more time to get used to the regime and to ensure compliance with it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My colleague from Hougang single member constituency, Dennis Tan, had earlier and also during the 2024 Committee of Supply, raised concerns too that the proposed six kilometre per hour speed limit appears to be tied to the average walking speed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This may be too slow and end up increasing the journey time for users and those who are reliant on it to move beyond their immediate neighbourhoods and also may have actual financial impact on those who rely on PMAs for their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could the Minister of State thus provide more specific details about how the new speed limit was arrived at?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is a similar issue with other reports, like the Panel's Review of Active Mobility Regulations for safer path sharing, which introduced the 10 kilometre per hour speed limit on footpaths, which I understand is based largely on work with focus groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While such focus groups are important for understanding these issues in Singapore's urban and cultural context, we must also engage with the research material, given that we regulate primarily for safety rather than more subjective concerns.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should understand how the science factors into these recommendations and I ask whether the panel should be updated to include more representation from academia.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also hope that future reviews of regulations would be driven primarily by research and that this research is communicated together with any proposed new regulations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: PMAs are useful to persons with disabilities and seniors by supporting their mobility in our communities and neighbourhoods, and can be important tools for removing barriers to accessing public transport.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They bring significant co-benefits in the form of promoting connections within the community, sociability, improving health and offering mobility, all with much lower carbon emissions than cars.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is a timely and necessary Bill that strengthens our transport regulatory framework amid evolving user behaviours, new mobility devices and rapid technological change.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The amendments relating to PMAs and PMDs, ERP 2.0 and road safety reflect a forward-looking effort to keep our public spaces safe and our system trusted.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These encounters may not make the headlines, but they shape how safe residents feel in our estates.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And when it comes to our common spaces and roads, safety cannot be optional.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, misuse and unsafe behaviour remain deep concerns.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Most users are responsible, but it only takes a few unsafe acts to undermine public trust and confidence for everyone.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These affect not just riders, but pedestrians, families and entire communities.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, while the Bill rightly strengthens the enforcement tools and registration requirements, I suggest that we consider a more graduated and targeted approach to penalties, especially for repeat offenders who knowingly disregard safety rules.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is really not about being harsh but rather being clear, consistent and protective, particularly for those who are vulnerable.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, to complement device identification, I propose we could explore a simple and visible rider identification system, especially for mobility devices issued for medical needs.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This would help enforcement officers act with confidence, while reassuring the public that these devices are being used legitimately.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to speak briefly on the healthcare implications of the proposed Certificate of Medical Need.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As a practising doctor, I support the intent to ensure that mobility devices and scooters are meant for those who need it and are directed to those who genuinely require them.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This protects public safety and preserves trust in the system.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Not too long ago, a Member in this House spoke about the effects of sarcopenia and aged-related muscle loss.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If our seniors and individuals who are actually physically able to walk end up using these devices, they could inadvertently lose their muscle mass and increase the risk of frailty in our community.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, we should be mindful of the practical impact on healthcare professionals and patients, especially those with temporary mobility limitations, such as individuals recovering from surgery, fractures, strokes or acute illnesses.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: After all, a safety framework works best when it protects patients without overwhelming clinics.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I encourage closer collaboration with healthcare providers as this framework is implemented.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Next, on the ERP 2.0 and the trust-based enforcement that ensues.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This reflects a mature regulatory approach that recognises that most cases of non-payment are due to administrative oversight rather than intentional evasion.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With the new penalty model, the Government reinforces trust with motorists while maintaining accountability.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If there is one area where we should continue to strengthen our approach, it is in addressing dangerous, negligent or reckless driving that results in serious injury or even loss of life.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When harm is irreversible, our sentencing framework must reflect that gravity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A calibrated approach would reinforce our national commitment to safety.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It tightens PMA regulation, introduces a trust-based approach to ERP 2.0 and modernises enforcement in meaningful ways.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The suggestions that I have raised on calibrated deterrence, visible identification, charging safety and healthcare-sensitive certification are offered in the spirit of strengthening safety while ensuring fairness and compassion.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: With these observations, I support the Bill and look forward to the Minister's response.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, to MOT on the keeping of unsafe devices under the Small Motorised Vehicle Safety Act, and secondly, to MHA on the proposed outsourcing of traffic violations processing under the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, let me say that I strongly support this amendment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From time to time, I have encountered AMD fires in my ward caused by overnight charging of devices suspected to have non-compliant batteries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The damage caused is not just to property, but also to residents of nearby units who suffer from smoke inhalation injury, such as swollen eyes and respiratory airways, and carbon monoxide poisoning.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Long after the fire subsides, residents look on AMDs at the common areas with trepidation, for fear that the next fire outside their door might leave them trapped.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nationwide, the effect of AMD fires has also been sobering.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On 12 January, in response to an Adjournment Motion filed by Workers' Party's Non-Constituency Member of Parliament Andre Low, MHA confirmed that AMD fires have been disproportionately fatal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The media release on this Bill by MOT also acknowledged that non-compliant e-scooters pose severe fire risk.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given this experience, I would expect LTA to take the lead in enforcement actions against non-compliant devices, especially those found at HDB blocks, where harm to many residents is most imminent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would thus be useful for MOT to clarify how enforcement actions will change when the Bill becomes law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Based on correspondence with LTA in July last year, I was given to understand that LTA's enforcement then was focused on non-compliant devices that were being ridden on public paths.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This was a point alluded to by the Minister of State in his speech earlier as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our Town Council was told that for non-compliant devices parked at common areas, the Town Council should do its own enforcement or review its bylaws, but clearly, Town Councils are not the subject matter experts as to whether a device is compliant or not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Two days ago, LTA had indicated to our Town Council its openness to including one of our hotspots in a possible island-wide operation against non-compliant AMDs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I welcome the Minister of State's statement earlier also, that under this Bill, the LTA's role will be enlarged in enforcement, in this area.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, Sir, with the amendments proposed today, could MOT confirm that LTA will be taking the lead in the enforcement of the new provisions in the common areas of HDB estates?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was stated that such a move would enable the Traffic Police to outsource the processing of straightforward cases and hence, free up resources to focus on more complex cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I have four queries that I would like the Ministry to clarify.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, it was mentioned that the outsourcing will be to civilian contractors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These civilian contractors are presumably private sector companies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What are the criteria for selection of these contractors?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will there be more than one contractor appointed concurrently?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry clarify at what level of detail these assessment frameworks will be pitched?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A case example using a specific offence would be useful to understand this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, residents may wish lodge appeals for offences to be waived or reduced.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although camera-detected violations might seem straightforward and not appealable, I have not found this to be true in all cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in one case, a resident of mine was initially charged with beating a red light.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After appealing to the Police, the charge was reduced to a lesser one of not forming up correctly when making a right turn, which carried a lower fine and less demerit points.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will the contractors similarly make such arrangements when requested?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, Sir, in summary, while I support the Bill, I look forward to the clarifications from the two Ministries.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I stood alongside neighbours during chaotic moments of evacuation, offering immediate aid and a listening ear.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In one of these fires, we faced the ultimate tragedy – the loss of two of our own residents.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Post fires, residents shared insecurities of living in their own homes.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One major concern involved living near neighbours with AMDs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I filed a total of 16 questions across MOT, MHA and MTI, because one fire is a fire too many, especially in what is supposed to be a safe abode.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And it is given this context that I respond to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I rise in support of the Bill and commend its decisive measures to improve the safety of our public paths and roads for all.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In particular, it addresses common concerns of Singaporeans about the misuse of PMAs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: By strengthening enforcement powers against AMDs, the Bill ensures safer roads, fairer usage of transport infrastructure and more sustainable mobility for all.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To better aid enforcement and implementation of the Bill, and to support vulnerable demographics that may be impacted, I would like to raise four points of clarification for the Ministry's consideration.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, there is a need to complement the implementation of the new regulations with community education to avoid inadvertent violations by genuine PMA users, particularly on the new rules regarding medical certification and registration.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some users, such as the elderly, are already not familiar with existing regulations.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For instance, the AMAP noted during their focused group discussions, that several participants were confused about the distinction between PMAs and PMDs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This points to a potential gap between legislative intent and user awareness.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thus, changes brought about in this Bill must be communicated effectively to ensure compliance.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, some of the changes introduced requires active steps to be taken by existing PMA users, such as visiting their healthcare provider for a certification that they are eligible to use or registering and obtaining an identification mark for their PMA.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Genuine users have raised concerns and questions as to what this will entail.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can these groups, particularly the elderly, be supported in navigating changes such as obtaining medical certification and registering their PMAs, in time before the enforcement of the new rules?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My second question relates to the disposal of non-compliant PMAs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill introduces new size and design requirements of a PMA, such as requiring it to only have one seat and to not exceed the maximum dimensions stated.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that the Bill will also make it illegal to keep unsafe devices at home and those who currently possess non-compliant PMAs will have to dispose of it.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moreover, to incentivise early disposal, registered owners who stepped forward for disposal qualified for an early disposal incentive.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Separately, weeks before etomidate was classified as a Class C illegal drug, the "Bin the Vape" Campaign offered a form of amnesty period – voluntary, no-questions-asked disposal of vape devices and related products.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My third point relates to the enforcement and implementation of speed limits.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I support this move, as it better reflects the intended use of PMAs to replace walking for users with mobility challenges.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For vehicles on the road, there are cameras to track when vehicles go past the speed limit.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will the Ministry also install similar cameras along walkways and shared paths to ensure that errant PMAs are properly fined for speeding offences?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While members of the public may report incidents of errant device users on public paths to LTA, it is more often difficult to do so practically.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Similar to how the Police and NEA has volunteers with enforcement powers, will the Ministry consider empowering LTA volunteers instead to check on PMA licences?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Enforcement of the new rules should not just focus on the behaviour of PMA users in our communities, but actions should also be considered to be taken against retailers and sellers of these non-compliant PMAs and illegal PMDs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this vein, I would like to clarify whether the Ministry will move beyond physical patrols to collaborating with community marketplaces, like Carousell, to automatically flag and delist these devices, and whether a proactive social media monitoring unit or public whistle-blowing mechanism will be established to identify users and retailers of modified devices.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How does the Ministry intend to address the issue of platform workers who currently use PMAs for food delivery, who are concerned that the lowered speed limit would affect the number of deliveries they can make and their livelihoods directly?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Platform workers are a valued part of the Singapore workforce, many of them work tirelessly to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Does the Ministry have plans to work together with platform operators like Grab and Foodpanda, to introduce initiatives that will ease the burden of the impact of new regulations on their livelihoods?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that the bulk of these fires occurred from devices that were illegally modified, or those that were not tested and certified.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This highlights the significance of robust fire safety standards and enforcement measures.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These comprehensive measures have undoubtedly prevented many fires and greatly improved the safety of AMDs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, the fire risk posed by PMAs is no less serious than that posed by PMDs and PABs.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Furthermore, PMAs are used by individuals like seniors with walking difficulties, who may not be able to escape to safety without substantial assistance in the event of a fire.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For this vulnerable demographic, fire regulations should be even more stringent, as commensurate with the increased vulnerabilities of the persons involved.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Considering the potentially long wait for an internationally recognised fire standard for PMAs to be established, I call upon the Ministry to strengthen fire regulations for PMAs with periodic inspections.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Transport safety does not begin only at home.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It does start the moment we step on the road too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It begins at home with our families, our neighbours and the choices we make in shared spaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Electric-powered PMDs have gained popularity as an affordable and efficient means of travel for many.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, these devices also pose higher fire risks in our homes and neighbourhoods.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As such, fires are often more severe and more likely to result in serious injuries and fatalities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is why Singapore has placed strong emphasis on the use of PMDs that comply with UL2272 fire safety standards.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Even so, improper use of unsafe charging practices can still pose significant risk to device owners, family members, neighbours and of course, our firefighters.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A firefighter once shared with me that the e-scooter battery fires are unlike the typical fires that they face.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They can reignite, generate intense heat and spread rapidly, especially in confined spaces.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The most distressing moments are when families are trapped behind close doors while corridors are filled with toxic smoke from burning lithium ion batteries.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I, the,refore commend our Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) officers for continuously upskilling our firefighters to respond to fires involving PMDs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But at the same time, prevention must remain our first line of defence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I urge all owners to check their devices and to use only UL2272-certified models to protect the safety of themselves and their loved ones.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And in a neighbourhood where we all live together, it is especially important that we remain vigilant and support each other in such a manner.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In land scarce Singapore, pedestrians and device users must share our limited space.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When accidents occur, the consequences can be serious, especially for elderly pedestrians who often sustain even more severe injuries and take much longer to recover.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I recall when I was a grassroots leader in Pasir Ris many years ago, I was distraught at the thought and sight of an elderly lady being hit by an e-scooter.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While these regulatory changes aim to improve pedestrian safety, which I really support, you must recognise that PMDs are medical devices that support persons with mobility impairments too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, for many PMDs like those in my constituency, which is aged and we have many elderly residents, PMDs are not merely a means of transport but an essential enabler for independence and dignity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They allow my residents to move about in their neighbourhoods, attend medical appointments, purchase daily necessities and manage personal errands independently.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I therefore call on the Ministry to implement these regulations in a manner that does not place additional burden or hardships on those with genuine needs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In particular, Sir, I seek clarification on whether assessments for the Certificate of Medical Need can be conducted at polyclinics so as to help manage costs and ensure accessibility.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: More than 6,000 cases involve lorries and other heavy vehicles.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When I was an SCDF officer many years ago, I witnessed an accident where a lorry was hit and the workers who were in the vehicle were thrown all over the road.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the site of that, being a part of the SCDF team, it just reminds me that we cannot allow these things to happen.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I really support this part of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the same time, I ask whether the Ministry is studying the challenges companies may face, whether cost, operational or technical to ensure that enforcement is effective and sustainable.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The PMA enables him to leave home independently, buy food, go for medical appointments and manage daily needs without relying entirely on family members.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: He moves slowly, carefully and complies with regulations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: His concern is not about safety, but about access – whether the process and cost of obtaining a Certificate of Medical Need will complicate something that is essential to his daily life.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a matter of shared values and responsibility.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When mobility devices are not safely stored or charged, the risk falls not only on one individual but on the entire family as well as neighbours around them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Fire and smoke know no boundaries of housing units.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: On the issue of PMAs, we must be clear that these devices are medical necessities for individuals with mobility constraints.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Rather, it is a device for independent living, for mobility and for continuing to contribute to as a member of society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many PMA users are also our platform workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Fair safety is safety that takes into account the reality of workers' lives.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Protecting lives, without denying the dignity of work and the right to earn a living.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When we care for the most vulnerable, the families, the senior citizens, persons with disabilities and workers, we are building a society that is safer, more humane and more resilient.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I rise to speak on the Certificate of Medical Need for driving or riding mobility vehicles.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: My team and I know who they are.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Her knees have given way, but her spirit has not.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: She still wants to go to the market, she still wants to choose her vegetables.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The uncle who has lost his leg to diabetes.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: He is not asking for pity, he is asking to get around.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Six months ago he was walking, now he is learning to live differently.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: These are the people this provision is meant to protect.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The first two are practical, the third is a reflection.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: A certificate is only as good as the assessment behind it and an assessment is only as good as the information available to the assessor.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: When a resident needs a Certificate of Medical Need, my advice is simple: see their regular doctor, their family physician, their enrolled Healthier SG clinic.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: They have watched the residents' mobility change over time.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: They understand the home environment, the daily routine, their goals, their values.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: That is the doctor best place to certify need.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I therefore ask that public messaging reinforces this clearly, not just see a doctor, but see your doctor.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: And for those who do not yet have a regular doctor to enrol into Healthier SG, start building their relationship.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It will serve them well, not just for this, but for their health over the long term.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: For those already using scooters and unsure if they qualify, we should encourage them to have an honest conversation with their doctor.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: For some, this may be the first medical review in years.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Conditions change, some may have improved, some may benefit from intervention.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This is not just certification, it is an opportunity for care.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: And for those who may not qualify, our role is to help them understand their options, including alternatives that may serve them better.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: We are not starting from zero, but clinical practice will surface grey zones conditions that do not fit neatly.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Residents whose function fluctuates, residents whose needs are hard to access in a clinic room.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Consider the resident in her 60s who can walk but has fallen three times this year.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: She is not immobile, but is she safe?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: These are the cases that do not fit neatly into "yes" or "no".

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Without clear guidance, different doctors may reach different conclusions and residents may learn to shop around.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Consistency protects both the resident and the system.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: For some of these cases, we welcome the option to tap on our occupational therapists.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: They assess function where it matters: in the home, on the path, in real life.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: That said, we will need supplementary guidance over time, learning from real cases, refining our approach.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I ask that the Ministry gathers feedback after roll-out and convenes sessions where practitioners can learn from case studies.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Medical Association's guidelines on medical assessment of fitness to drive is a good model.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: These consultations may be difficult, especially when a resident wants a scooter but does not qualify.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But this is not new to us, we navigate these conversations every day.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I encourage my fellow clinicians to approach these assessments with confidence.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: These are opportunities for meaningful conversation to understand our residents' needs, review their conditions and help them move forward safely.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: They serve those who needed them, often under funding safeguards that ensured appropriate use.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But as these devices became commercially available, usage grew far beyond the intended population.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: And now, we respond with certification, with healthcare as gatekeepers.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I understand why this response is necessary and I credit the Ministry for consulting the professional bodies and developing guidelines before roll-out.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But I ask the Government: how did we get here, reacting downstream instead of having built in safeguards upstream from the start?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Healthcare will do her part for public safety and the public good.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But let me name what such a reactive policy costs.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: In the meantime, there will be workarounds, goodwill, clinicians doing what needs to be done.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Workarounds in our systems, goodwill is not infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The question now is: how do we avoid being here again?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This is not the first time across-Ministry policy has landed at healthcare door.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: So, I say this: continue to consult healthcare at design.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: We know what good design looks like, driving licensed medical assessments where verification is needed before you drive, work permit medical examinations where clearance is needed before the permit, disabled parking labels, where need is verified upfront.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: These systems work because they are tied upstream with verification built in from the start.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: For mobility scooters, the gap was the commercial market.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Pegged with healthcare certificate or medical need, this creates a system that is tight at entry.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This is good design and I welcome it.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Let us set up this policy well for them.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The assessors, let us continue refining our guidelines and supporting our clinicians and occupational therapists to do their work with confidence and let us learn from this for what may come next.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thus, I appreciate Minister of State Baey's acknowledgment of the Bill's attempt to balance access and safety.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Both access and safety are critical for this freedom that mobility offers us.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Under this Bill, pedestrians have freedom from injury and neighbours, freedom from PMD-related fires.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And the gracious use of our transport system helps to increase this sense of freedom.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Recently, I met with parents of young children together with my fellow Group Representation Constituency MP Cai Yinzhou, to hear about their struggles on commuting, whether it is carrying strollers onto public buses or whether they are fearful of sharing paths with fast-moving personal mobility devices.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a mother myself who takes public transport, I completely understand the struggle.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is built on a social compact and understanding that we move through the city as members of one community, not merely as separate individuals seeking to reach our destinations.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to show grace, patience and kindness to one another as we travel together.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Bill addresses three critical areas where that graciousness is tested.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The amendments to mobility scooters and PMAs do not punish disabled persons.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They protect them and they protect our shared spaces.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Able-bodied individuals operating mobility devices unsuitable for pedestrian paths have created genuine hazards for the elderly and young children.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The measures proposed – requiring medical certification, reducing speed limits and establishing device registration – serve to ensure that those with genuine needs can move safely and with dignity.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When someone who cannot walk risks collision because an able-bodied person misuses a scooter, this affects the community.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When an oversized device occupies space meant for a young child, the dignity of the disabled user is compromised alongside the safety of others.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Good regulation is an expression of grace toward all, including our disabled citizens.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It communicates that all our needs are real, that our dignity is protected and those around us will be safer when sharing space with us.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The speed limiter, amendments for lorries between 3.5 and 12 tonnes will reduce road fatalities and protect our communities.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The same can be said for PMDs without UL2272, which remain fire hazards.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thirdly, regarding the ERP 2.0 system and the decriminalisation of charges.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This change reflects a mature, refined approach to accountability.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Vehicle owners will face real consequences, helping us to ensure compliance without the bluntness of criminal prosecution.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These measures protect the community by ensuring that those who use our roads do so responsibly and the enforcement mechanisms serve the broader good.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They are all expressions of a single principle: when we use shared transport infrastructure, we do so as members of a community, not in isolation.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That community comprises the elderly gentleman on a mobility scooter, the young mother with a child, or a lorry driver navigating a residential area, the casual road user and all of us who depend on moving safely through Singapore.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Graciousness does not mean the absence of rules.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Graciousness means rules that protect the vulnerable while serving the legitimate needs of all.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As this Bill moves towards debate and implementation, I wish to invite all members of our community to consider two commitments.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, a commitment to graciousness towards the young, disabled and elderly persons on our transport systems – the people whom we should be looking out for.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is recognition of the equal standing in our community.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They deserve the same freedoms that we enjoy, the same access to the transport infrastructure that we use and the same dignity as we commute together.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One of my volunteers also shared about a time when he was unable to enter a lift after waiting 15 minutes even though he had a young child in a stroller with him.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This was because the lift was full of able-bodied commuters.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He eventually had to take the escalator even though it posed a safety risk.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I encourage members of the public to show graciousness towards them and others like them to understand that the disabled person on a mobility scooter, navigating a crowded path, or an elderly uncle lumbering on a public sidewalk are not obstacles to go around, but people exercising their right to move independently.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As our city becomes busier, the noise in our environment, where the buses, trains, stations or footpaths has deteriorated.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Noise is a form of pollution that affects the well-being of all commuters, particularly the elderly and those with sensory sensitivities.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Transport operators and enforcement officers should be empowered to enforce reasonable conduct standards.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Accordingly, Mr Deputy Speaker, I commend this Bill to the House.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I rise in support of this amendment Bill and its intent to improve safety on our public paths, reduce fire risks from unsafe devices and strengthen accountability in the personal mobility space.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I will be addressing the active mobility provisions in my clarification and I would like to frame my comments around three topics: first, users and their caregivers; second, consistent enforcement; and lastly, device safety, storage and the role of our community.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It ensures PMAs are used appropriately and by those who genuinely need them.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But on the ground, situations are rarely black and white.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: A resident in my Naval Base constituency is medically weak due to multiple complications and relies on her husband to accompany her on her PMD.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In another case, a couple shared that the wife would ride the PMD after the husband completes his dialysis as he is too weak to do so himself.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: They are concerned that such arrangements may now face penalties under the new framework.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Under the existing Active Mobility Act 2017, a "mobility scooter" is defined to mean a vehicle that has a seat and is designed to carry a single individual.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Arguably, it does not extend to a scooter that is designed for two persons, for example, where a caregiver rides the scooter with an incapacitated pillion rider.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Taken together, these provisions leave open the possibility that certain vehicles, such as the two-seater vehicles that I have mentioned as an example, being prescribed as mobility vehicles and permitted for use under certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Would the Ministry further study such practical needs when developing the subsidiary legislation?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: There may be circumstances where it may be necessary or convenient for an incapacitated individual and his caregiver to use a two-seater vehicle for legitimate mobility purposes, for example, if the individual is exhausted from dialysis or otherwise temporarily incapacitated from operating the vehicle.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: While enforcers may exercise discretion, policy clarity gives confidence to families and certainty to enforcement officers.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In addition, I would like to ask: one, how does the Ministry to balance the risk of "assessor shopping" with the provision of avenues for applicants to seek a second opinion in good faith?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Two, what are the proposed timelines from application to clinical assessment and issuance of the certificate?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: And three, how will the Ministry ensure that fees are affordable?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: For example, would individuals with permanent and irreversible medical conditions be granted certificates with an indefinite validity period to minimise the inconvenience of periodic renewals?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Residents recovering from surgery, fractures, stroke, chemotherapy or dialysis may only need a mobility scooter for a few weeks or months, not permanently.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, I note that clause 16 of the Amendment Bill introduces a new section 23K of the Active Mobility Act, which contemplates that each certificate will have a validity period.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: So, I would like to ask: will the framework allow for short-duration certificates and can validity periods be proportionate to medical need, instead of a fixed renewal cycle?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Ultimately, clarity on the form of the certificates would be helpful as this avoids over-medicalising temporary conditions and repeated clinic visits for residents who are already unwell.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Furthermore, PMAs will now be required to carry registration marks which allow for enforcement.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Recently, LTA installed a temporary enforcement camera right outside Canberra Primary School.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: However, residents were surprised when it was removed after just three weeks.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: So, I would like to ask, can LTA publish clearer criteria on where cameras are likely be deployed, for how long and what conditions trigger removal or extension?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Visibility of such cameras builds trust and acts as an effective deterrent and assures road users that we are doing our best to keep our roads and pathways safe for all.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: My suggestion is to consider permanent cameras at school zones, downward slopes and high foot-traffic areas; temporary cameras to rotate between key junctions and supported by roving enforcement elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: While PMDs are still in its nascency in Singapore, it is consistency in enforcement that will likely change behaviour.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Should there be a lack of resources or funding for such permanent cameras, could we also explore a co-funding model between local Town Councils and LTA for estates which want to participate in enforcement?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Making it an offence to keep unsafe devices is necessary.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Fire risks are real, and we have seen tragic consequences.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Under the Active Mobility Act, there is already provision for authorised officers and public path wardens, including volunteers.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Enforcement exists today, but residents' feedback that coverage and visibility can feel uneven, especially at hotspots.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: My question is, can MOT and LTA expand the use of this existing framework to educate, identify high-risk devices and prevent incidents early?

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: For example, strengthening public path warden presence, partnering Town Councils and Community Emergency and Engagement (C2E) Committees and empowering our Active Mobility Community Ambassadors (AMCA).

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Today, residents can already report illegal vehicle parking through OneMotoring.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: So, I would like to suggest for MOT to explore a similar structured reporting channel, perhaps through OneService, for PMD and PMA issues.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: For example, uploading your photo, tagging your location and simple categorisation.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This will allow for faster response, active community eyes on the ground and early detection of unsafe devices.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: It strengthens safety without over-reliance on enforcement alone.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: As the Government has noted previously, although AMD-related fires form a small proportion of fires in HDB estates, such fires are typically more severe and more likely to result in fatalities and injuries.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: While registration and the requirement for devices to be UL2272-compliant are useful in reducing the risk of fires, they do not adequately address the fire risk of compliant devices.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Alternatively, we could consider sandboxes in MSCPs where usage is low.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This idea is not plucked out from thin air.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I deal with batteries on a daily basis and last Saturday, also had a chat with a retailer on the sideline of our fire safety talk.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, they agreed that with three to four connectors head and three to four voltages, the permutation is not that many for such a sandbox to be deployed quickly.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I would like to briefly present my views in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This amendment Bill is heading in the right direction, but the real key lies in how to implement the policy effectively.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: This system is heading in the right direction, but real life is often more complex than legal provisions.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: In the community, there are many elderly people who are temporarily weak after dialysis, chemotherapy or surgery, and need family members or caregivers to assist them in using mobility aids.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I hope the policy can provide clear guidance so that caregivers do not have to worry about enforcement risks in reasonable circumstances.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, we also see many residents who are only temporarily mobility-impaired, such as after surgery or fracture.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I hope the system can allow short-term or time-limited medical certificates, whilst for permanent medical conditions, consideration could be given to longer validity periods which needs less frequent updating, to reduce the burden of repeated medical consultations for patients.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Taking school areas as an example, if enforcement is only short-term, it easily creates a mentality of "things will be fine once the attention dies down".

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I hope the authorities can clearly explain the deployment principles for speed cameras and consider establishing permanent enforcement points at high-risk locations, with roving enforcement in other areas, to give the public a stable sense of security.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: The registration system is important, but for many elderly people, digital processes are not user-friendly.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: If registration responsibility could be moved forward to points of sale, ensuring compliance from the source, this would both reduce pressure on the elderly and lower subsequent enforcement costs.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: Regarding fire prevention, even compliant equipment still poses certain risks.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I hope the Government can study setting up fire-resistant charging or parking solutions in HDB multi-storey car parks and, through pilot testing, further reduce threats to residents' lives and property.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: As long as the policy can truly accommodate family needs, be feasible for businesses and allow community participation, this Bill can achieve a better balance between safety and inclusiveness. : Sir, this Bill sets the right direction.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: But laws succeed only when families feel supported, users and companies can comply and communities feel safe.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: My intent today is to help make this policy work better on the ground.

speaker: Mr Ng Shi Xuan (Sembawang)
text: I look forward to the Minister's clarifications and how we can refine implementation together.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Land Transport and Related Matters Bill is important for its impact on safeguarding lives and preparing our transport system for the future.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Where genuine difficulties exist, can more assistance be rendered?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Safety should never be compromised because of affordability or administrative hurdles.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Between 2022 and 2025, over 70% of such fires involved uncertified or illegally modified devices.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bill rightly prohibits even the possession of non-UL2272 e-scooters.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With thousands of devices in circulation and illegal spare parts easily available online, accountability must extend beyond users to the platforms that enable such risks.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The question before us is this: how can enforcement be scaled sustainably across our estates?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How can agencies work with communities to build awareness and vigilance?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And how can we ensure that online marketplaces take responsibility, so that unsafe devices are not just removed from our paths but from our homes altogether?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: PMAs are essential for those with genuine walking difficulties.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But misuse by otherwise mobile individuals can create new problems.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Over-reliance on mobility scooters may lead to muscle wasting, loss of balance and reduced independence.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Instead of preserving mobility, unnecessary use can erode it.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is why the prescription requirement, through a Certificate of Medical Need issued by doctors or occupational therapists, is so important.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It ensures that PMAs remain tools of necessity, not convenience, protecting both the safety of our shared paths and the health of our residents.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It directly addresses concerns in towns with young children and seniors.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Dimension limits of 120 centimetres by 70 centimetres, harmonised with public transport standards, will prevent oversized devices from dominating shared paths.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Yet, enforcement on the ground remains the challenge.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Tengah, residents have raised concerns about riders whizzing past pedestrians, with near-miss collisions involving young children along Plantation Plaza's retail street.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With our ageing population, we can expect more PMAs on our paths too.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Doctors provide the vital role of diagnosis, ensuring medical conditions are properly identified.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Physiotherapists, however, are the movement experts, the mobility experts.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They specialise in biomechanics, gait analysis and functional rehabilitation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As part of their work, they prescribe wheelchairs and mobility aids for persons with disabilities, and they work daily with patients to help restore movement – to stand, to walk and to carry out their ADLs with dignity and independence.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For residents already under physiotherapy care, requiring a separate doctor consultation for certification may create duplication and inconvenience.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For continuity of care, patients already receiving physiotherapy should not require separate consultations solely for certification purposes.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Doctors diagnose, but physiotherapists help people move again – to stand, to walk and to live.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, while these measures improve safety, infrastructure remains a concern.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Shared paths of two metres are dwarfed by roads spanning 18 metres.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If active mobility is to grow, will the Government commit to expanding pedestrian‑only path infrastructure proportionately?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Safety is not just about rules; it is also about space.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: ERP 2.0 represents a fairer, usage-based model, charging only for actual road use.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But fairness must be felt across income groups and vehicle types.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will lower‑income families who rely on private‑hire vehicles for essential transport be protected from disproportionate burdens under future distance‑based models?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And while decriminalising missed payments is sensible, shifting liability from drivers to vehicle owners may create complications for shared vehicles.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But as always, the true measure lies in implementation, in enforcement, in fairness and in infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support the Bill and I look forward to the Minister's clarifications.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I would like to seek clarifications from the Minister of State on several implementation matters that will affect our residents and businesses.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The new regulation requiring valid medical certification for mobility scooters is necessary.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It addresses legitimate public concerns about misuse by able-bodied individuals and preserves these devices for those with genuine mobility challenges.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: I do so not only as a Member of this House, but as someone like many Singaporeans who uses our transport system every day – walking through neighbourhoods, sharing footpaths and relying on our roads and common spaces to feel safe and predictable.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Transport policy may be debated here, but its impact is felt outside this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It is felt on our footpaths, in lift lobbies and in the confidence that people have when they move around their neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: In that sense, this Bill is not just technical or administrative.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It is about how we update our rules to reflect how people live today, while continuing to keep everyone safe and included.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Over the past years, many Members would have seen reports of mobility devices colliding with pedestrians, or fires linked to unsafe or modified devices stored in residential blocks.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Not because mobility aids are the problem – they are not.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But because they show that our rules have not fully kept up with how these devices are being used and sometimes misused, in shared public spaces.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Mobility devices today are more powerful and more widely available than before.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: If used properly, they make a real difference to people's lives.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
