text: If used irresponsibly or without safeguards, they can pose risks to others.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill is timely in addressing that gap.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: They recognise that many seniors and persons with disabilities, these devices are not conveniences.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: They are essential tools that allow people to remain independent, mobile and connected to the community.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, the Bill reinforces an important principle: our footpaths and common spaces are shared.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: As devices become faster or heavier, greater responsibility must follow.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Clear rules protect pedestrians, but they also protect responsible users who rely on these devices and do not want to be unfairly judged because of the actions of a few.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: When I speak with residents, the concern is rarely about seniors who truly need these aids.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: And if something goes wrong, who is accountable?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: When there is uncertainty, trust in shared spaces begins to erode.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Seniors navigating medical assessments, online systems or registration processes should not feel anxious or overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: I encourage the Ministry to continue pairing regulation with strong outreach through community centres, healthcare providers and grassroots organisations, especially during the transition period.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Too often, enforcement falls mainly on end-users, even when powerful devices are marketed without proper safeguards or clear information.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: By placing clearer responsibility on sellers and platforms, the Bill improves accountability and sends a clear message that safety must be built in from the start.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Related to this are the provisions dealing with unsafe devices, including those that are modified or uncertified.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Many of us will recall reports of fires in residential blocks linked to such devices.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: These incidents are frightening because they do not affect just one household.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: They put neighbours, families and the entire block at risk.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, I welcome the reasonable-excuse safeguards and transitional arrangements.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Too often, attention comes only after something bad happen – when lives are lost or permanently changed.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Clearer statutory guidance strengthens deterrence, while still allowing Judges the discretion to respond fairly to the seriousness of each case.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: The enhanced speed limiter regime for heavy vehicles is also timely.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: When safeguards are bypassed, the harm caused can be severe and irreversible.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Tightening these controls reflects lessons learned through experience and reinforces our commitment to road safety.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: From speed cameras to electronic charging systems, technology now plays a central role in transport management.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill updates evidentiary and enforcement provisions to reflect this reality.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: But even as systems become more efficient, it is important that people continue to have access to clear explanations and meaningful recourse.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Systems must not only work well, they must also be fair, transparent and understandable.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has always done well because people trust that our systems are designed with care, applied proportionately and corrected when they fall short.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill helps to maintain that trust by modernising our laws while keeping people at the centre.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It is about responding responsibly to technological, demographic and social change.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It seeks to protect seniors, support mobility, improve safety and modernise enforcement, without losing sight of fairness and common sense.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Preventing the misuse of PMAs by seemingly able-bodied individuals, tackling speeding and restricting the use of overly large devices, are good proposals by the AMAP and I am glad that the Government has adopted these recommendations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must not compromise the safety of other path users, especially seniors and young children, when allowing AMDs to share our paths.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond the measures proposed, I would like to urge the Government to do more to tackle the occurrences of fires caused by these AMDs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In my Radin Mas constituency, I have seen our fair share of fires caused by PMDs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I understand that some of these fires were due to the use of unapproved PMDs, or in some cases, modifications to battery packs to improve the devices' range.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In addition to endangering themselves, the owners of unapproved or illegally modified devices can cause harm to their neighbours in the event that these devices catch fire.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Electrical fires can spread far more rapidly and the damage to surrounding HDB flats also tend to be more excessive.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to a 2024 research article published in the Journal of Burn Care and Research, burn injuries related to lithium-ion batteries from PMDs can often be more severe than other types of burns, due to the thermal runway caused by such electrical fires.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The British Safety Council has also issued a warning that, once a chemical reaction causes thermal runway, the lithium-ion batteries found in these PMDs could spontaneously ignite and such fires are hard to extinguish.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This means that we do not need to be charging the batteries for them to catch fire.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must therefore do all we can to prevent people from possessing devices that have been illegally modified, due to the risk of devastating electrical fires that can result in the unfortunate loss of lives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I note that LTA had previously said that these gantries would be progressively removed once ERP 2.0 begins and I am wondering if the Minister could provide more information on the timeline.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Workers who travel extensively on our roads for their livelihoods, are rightfully concerned about the impact of distance-based congestion pricing that would be enabled by the ERP 2.0 system.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge the Ministry to consider in its implementation the disproportionate impact that distance-based congestion pricing would have on these workers and their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Those with outstanding payments would be unable to transact with LTA on some essential services, such as road tax renewal, until the missed ERP charges are settled.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, in the event where the vehicle owner fails to renew his road tax due to outstanding ERP payments, and the driver, who is an employee, is unaware of this and drives the vehicle, who would be liable for the resulting offence?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Should we therefore align the current framework to also hold the vehicle owner liable, instead of the driver?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I support the proposal to increase penalties for several road traffic offences, such as the illegal alteration of motor vehicles and taking to task those who allow illegal modifications to take place within their premises.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I also support the proposal to increase penalties for keeping or using unregistered or deregistered vehicles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Absent from the stipulated vehicle inspections, these unregistered or deregistered vehicles can pose a safety risk to other road users.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would therefore like to ask how many cases did the Police investigate regarding the use of unregistered or deregistered vehicles on our roads in the past three years and how do we intend to do better enforcement to catch the users of such non-registered vehicles?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can the ERP 2.0 system be used to monitor and locate these vehicles?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: And if so, would the Police be able to use this system, so that they can take prompt enforcement actions?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I therefore thank the two Ministries – MOT and MHA – for working on this comprehensive Bill to make our roads and shared paths safer for everyone.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, in my view, this omnibus Bill was a missed opportunity to strengthen legislation to improve workers' safety.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We have seen numerous traffic accidents involving workers being transported at the back of lorries happen over the years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Accidents like this remind us time and time again that more needs to be done to improve the safety of workers being transported at the back of lorries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: NTUC and the Migrant Worker Centre have previously called for clearer restrictions on the co-mingling of workers with goods.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Carrying passengers alongside goods and machinery is dangerous.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Ideally, we should use proper transportation, such as buses, to transport our workers to and from their worksites.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I therefore urge the Government to adopt these proposals because the lives of every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Government could consider my proposals to strengthen enforcement against unsafe deregistered vehicles from plying our roads and to improve the safety of workers, currently being transported at the back of lorries.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Public safety is of utmost importance and I welcome and support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Some of the measures introduced in this Bill, I feel are long overdue.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: While I share the same reservations with my Parliamentary colleagues, that this may penalise some PMA users, specifically those who make use of their device to make a living as platform delivery workers, I can understand this from a perspective of public policy.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I had raised a Parliamentary question on this issue previously and had an exchange with the hon Minister of State for Transport before.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I remember, I noted in that exchange that 25 kilometres per hour is essentially a fit person running at full throttle or sprinting all out.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: To give a more easily perceived perspective, that is about a 100-metre sprint in 14.4 seconds.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Indeed, I doubt that there is anyone in this House who could have done so.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And I know that there are some very fit Members in this House.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: And this reinforces my point – 25 kilometres per hour is a very fast speed on our shared paths.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The momentum of a person holding down at this speed on our shared paths, whether he be on two legs or a bicycle, or even a PMD, has the potential to make any accidents a serious and even a very deadly one.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Someone dashing and crashing into you at 25 kilometres per hour is no joking matter.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This is an issue in my ward, and I have received many residents feedback on speeding bicycles and SMVs in the Tanjong Rhu area.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our shared paths are used by many of our elderly residents, young children and even pets.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But in the same interest of public safety, I must also call on LTA to review the speed limit for these devices on our shared paths.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I am glad to know that expanded powers that will be given to LTA officers under this new Bill.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Currently, the active mobility act allows LTA enforcement officers to enter and inspect business premises suspected of committing offences, such as illegally modifying devices and selling non-compliant devices, and to seize such devices.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But yet, I cannot help but note that majority of the AMD-related fires occurred not in commercial and business premises but private residential homes.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Allow me to share a quote from Cesare Beccaria, one of the founding figures of modern criminology and criminal law, "Crimes are more effectively prevented by certainty than severity of punishment." While I am in no way equating possession of an illegal modified PMD to say rape and robbery, this truism is universally applicable.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Punishment and sanctions are only half of the deterrence, and the other half is the certainty of getting caught.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I commend the LTA wardens that I and my activists work at the Tanjong Rhu bridge.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But the problem we have with bicycles and PMDs persist despite their efforts.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Simply put, they could not be everywhere all the time.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Errant PMDs and PABs are still a sight in our neighbourhoods, especially at night.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For this Bill to be meaningful and to make our shared spaces safer, the enforcement efforts must be sustained, persistent and adequately resourced.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But I do not think that enforcement alone is enough to comprehensively address this issue.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: While enforcement is critical, we must also examine why risky behaviour persists.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Why do so many still obtain illegal devices, modify them and travel at unsafe speeds on our public paths?

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: So far, most of our previous efforts at addressing this problem have been focused on enforcement and the throttling of the supply of equipment.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We have not quite succeeded, otherwise we would not be here debating this Bill.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But it is certainly not for lack of trying.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I believe we did not succeed because we have never really addressed the root of what drives such unsafe behaviour.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is time that we address the elephant in the room.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Indeed, I believe performing platform delivery is the primary reason why people acquire these devices.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For these users, public and personal safety becomes not just an issue of personal responsibility but also systemic pressures.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In reality, platform riders operate under constant time pressures driven by targets, bonuses and performance-based incentives.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Earnings are linked to the number of orders completed, delivery speed and acceptance rates.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It also rises non-linearly, with significant jumps once certain quotas are met.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Platform riders are under pressure to hit these time limited quotas to substantially boost their earnings.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: For many of them, the only path to a viable income is by hitting these targets.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: This pressure cooker environment in which riders are driven to move faster and faster, under such models, speed and output are rewarded while safety is left to individual discretion.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: In this context, risky behaviour may not be explicitly encouraged, but it is effectively incentivised.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The Government enacts and enforces rules to protect public safety, including the safety of the rider themselves, yet the riders run the risk and bear the effect of these rules.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: The Government gets the blame for trying to keep everyone safe, meanwhile platform companies reap the rewards.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Public safety cannot be the Government's concern alone.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It is time to hold platform companies more accountable for the safety of their workers and the communities that they serve.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Without the delivery platform stepping up and taking greater responsibility, the powerful motivation and incentive to unsafe behaviour will always be present.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: It seems we have finally started to address the elephant in the room.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: But there is so much more that the platforms can do and should do.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: These simple measures could address much of the problem and platforms clearly have the means to significantly improve safety for both their riders and the public.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: They are stakeholders in the communities that they operate in.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We must recognise that safety on the roads and public paths is a shared responsibility.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: While the Government can make and enforce rules, platforms should ensure that their operational models do not systematically reward unsafe riding at the expense of public safety.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Their systems should protect their workers from unreasonable pressure and protect the public from unnecessary risk.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: At the same time, this must not become an excuse for platforms to shift responsibility or cost onto their workers.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our delivery workers deserve to be compensated fairly and sustainably.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: I look forward to hearing more about the outcome.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: Our delivery workers should not have to choose between earning a viable living and obeying the law and everyone deserves safety on our roads and public paths.

speaker: Ms Gho Sze Kee (Mountbatten)
text: We all deserve to return home safely to our loved ones at the end of the day.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hoped that through the session, my residents would develop a deeper understanding of our Parliamentary proceedings and a stronger sense of engagement viz these debates.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, after the Bill was tabled in Parliament for the First Reading in January, I met residents who responded to an open call for a full-day session on 17 January where we had robust and enriching discussions on the active mobility segments of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Following the session, the participants spent an additional week to co-develop a close to 60-page report synthesising our discussion and I will highlight the key points in the report in my speech today.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At they same time, they also raised several practical considerations and suggestions that were all people-centred, focused on the needs of fellow citizens with mobility challenges.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we would like to seek clarification from the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, there were concerns that different medical practitioners may have differing practices in ascertaining the need, so how will MOH ensure standardised clinical practice?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because on the one hand, we want to ensure that those with genuine mobility challenges are able to get the certification with minimum hassle.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But on the other hand, we also hope that in making the assessments, our practitioners do not inadvertently encourage the over-reliance on the mobility vehicles for those who are still able to move about relatively independently.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, the introduction of the need to register mobility vehicles.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We agree that this facilitates greater accountability and can help with enforcement as, currently, the lack of identification marks constrains enforcement even when offences may be detected by the Active Mobility Enforcement Cameras.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we would like to highlight that this may not fully address the challenge of enforcing against those who do not register and therefore, continue to run around without identification marks on their mobility vehicles.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, therefore, despite the changes in the legislation, adequate presence on the ground continues to remain critical to enforcing against this group.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, while we acknowledge the potential benefits of registration, several residents asked if the need to register would be too onerous for those with genuine medical need given that they would already have had to obtain the medical certificate and many of whom may be facing financial challenges.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We would also like to highlight one particular provision in the Act and seek clarification.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Specifically, why is an additional identification mark required at the registered responsible person's expense when there will already be a registration mark issued by LTA?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What information will be placed on the marks?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Several of my residents were particularly concerned about this.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will there be any personal data and privacy concerns as the marks may allow the public to identify people with mobility challenges based on the marks on the mobility vehicle alone even if nobody is using the vehicle?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will these modes still be allowed, as these could be more cost-effective options for those in need?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, the introduction of greater platform operator responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a good number of mobility vehicle users we encounter on the paths are delivery workers, we support these changes.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The secondary level of oversight placed on platform operators will complement the medical certificate requirement.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, we hope that these additional responsibilities do not lead to platform operators deciding to deprioritise or stop onboarding mobility vehicle users onto their platforms.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, with the lower allowable speeds of such vehicles, it is even more important that our platform operators continue to support those with mobility challenges as they seek to earn a livelihood.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this regard, I was very glad to hear Ms Yeo Wan Ling's update that the platform workers have been working very closely with NDCA and the union to ensure that this is done.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Fourth, the new rules on the selling and advertising of mobility vehicles.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We support commercial regulation as this helps to ensure upstream accountability.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We note, however, that the current Bill does not extend to regulating against the advertising of illegal repairs and modifications to mobility vehicles.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is the advertising of these illegal repairs.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is this an area that the Ministry intends to cover?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And finally, given that the intent is for mobility vehicles to only be used by those with mobility challenges, did the Ministry consider centralising the supply through healthcare institutions only, for example?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I support the reduction to six kilometres per hour, similar to Members like Mr Ng Shi Xuan.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And, in fact, it is not only Singapore that believes so.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And I think that is something that all Members so far have raised as of critical input to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, Mr Speaker, in closing, I would like to acknowledge the valuable input and perspectives of my residents on the Bill once again and I look forward to engaging them on more Bills, especially those under the Ministries that I am a GPC Member of – the Ministry of National Development, and the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment – as well as those impacting our built environment in general, such as this Bill, because it affects all of us.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Yesterday's debate covered a wide range of issues – from safety to enforcement and lived experience.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I hope to build on those contributions, beginning with my experience with enforcement on the ground before turning to specific provisions of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Just a couple of weeks ago, I witnessed a joint enforcement operation conducted by the Traffic Police, the National Environment Agency (NEA) and the Land Transport Authority (LTA) in the northeastern part of Singapore in Tampines East and Changi.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The operation took place between 2.00 am and 5.00 am.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While most Singaporeans were asleep, officers were out on the roads, conducting checks, managing risks and keeping our communities safe.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I and, I am sure, hon Member Dr Charlene Chen, would like to place on record our appreciation for these officers who work late nights, often unseen, so that our roads are safe.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: After I shared a short post about the experience, intended mainly for my residents, I was struck by the response from across Singapore, with many asking for more of such enforcements in their own neighbourhoods.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Singaporeans care deeply about road safety, public order and fair enforcement and they expect these to be applied consistently.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is in this context that the Land Transport and Related Matters Bill is timely.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Bill strengthens enforcement, clarifies powers and responds to realities on the ground.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I will touch on four areas: illegal vehicle modifications, Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) reforms, active mobility and speed limiters for lorries.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Across all four, the common thread is simple: rules must be clear, enforceable, credible and implementation is fair.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Clause 52 strengthens penalties for unauthorised modifications and this is necessary.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Excessively loud exhausts and unsafe aftermarket parts are not minor lifestyle choices.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They create safety risks, public nuisance and enforcement challenges.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And in Changi, residents regularly tell me how late-night noise from illegally modified vehicles disrupts sleep, affecting the elderly, young children and working adults.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This need to align policy with reality also applies to ERP 2.0.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I welcome the move to decriminalise missed ERP charges and treat them as administrative matters.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In an automated system, this avoids unnecessary criminalisation for what are often genuine technical lapses.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At the same time, accountability should be fair.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Holding vehicle owners liable in all cases may not reflect actual usage, particularly in legitimate shared-use contexts such as large families.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A more nuanced approach could better align responsibility with behaviour.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A motorcyclist in my constituency experienced a faulty On-Board Unit (OBU) that was initially eligible for a replacement.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: However, after a minor hairline crack was detected, he was required to bear the full replacement cost despite no major accident or misuse.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This raises questions about durability standards, especially in Singapore's climate.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Existing alerts on bus lanes and speed limits are useful.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Ministry could also explore further features such as alerts for flood-prone roads during heavy rain to support drivers.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: She suffered serious injuries, required jaw reconstruction surgery and continues to undergo follow-up care with the dentist and speech therapists.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This incident involved a PAB, even though this Bill focuses on personal mobility aids (PMAs).

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I raise it not to conflate device types but to highlight a fundamental reality – on shared paths, pedestrians bear the greatest risk when this risk is mismanaged.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Following the incident, Mr Frank Singam, Malar's husband, conducted a ground-up public survey which attracted over 600 responses.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The aim was not to centre in one case but to see if it reflected a broader pattern.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: There is strong rejection of fast-moving devices on pavements and an overwhelming view that pedestrian safety must come first.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: What is striking is that respondents are not calling for extreme measures.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They are just asking for three things: clear prioritisation of pedestrians, proper enforcement of existing rules and alignment between policy intent and daily experience.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: To work well, the process must be clear, accessible and affordable.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Excessive or opaque cost or administrative burden risks penalising genuine users.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A transparent appeal mechanism is also important, especially for temporary or borderline conditions.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Safeguards should protect the vulnerable and not overwhelm them.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Speed limits on shared paths matter only if they are enforced.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Public concern is less about the precise number – whether it is 10 or six – and more about excessive speed in crowded, high-risk areas.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Any speed limit, no matter how well designed, is meaningless if it is not enforced.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Several hon Members yesterday suggested permanent enforcement measures such as fixed cameras near schools, bus stops and high-traffic pedestrian areas.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Visible, location-focused enforcement supported by design-based speed calming is how speed limits move from policy intent to real safety.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Enforcement aside, it is also meaningless and unfair to users of PMAs who do not have speedometers for their own awareness of the speed they are going at in the first place.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Fire safety related to PMD- and PMA-charging remains a serious concern.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Designated charging and parking areas under residential blocks, also suggested by many hon Members yesterday, could reduce unsafe home charging while improving orderliness in shared spaces.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I had raised this issue through a Parliamentary Question in November 2025 and I thank the Minister for Home Affairs for his response.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A more targeted outreach and hands-on installation support could help smaller operators comply.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Using productivity grants for mandatory requirements risks diluting their purpose.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At its heart, it challenges all of us to improve safety without making daily life harder for those already trying to comply and do the right thing.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And to Mrs Malar Singam, I wish you a smoother path to full recovery.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Specifically, I welcome the Bill's active mobility provisions with respect to those on mobility devices and e-scooters.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is because in my role as a Member of Parliament (MP), I have received multiple emails from different Clementi residents about personal mobility devices (PMDs) travelling too fast on walkways, near misses and the anxiety this causes for pedestrians, especially for our seniors and our young children.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Furthermore, other residents in Clementi have also shared with me their concerns seeing seemingly able-bodied users riding oversized devices and also clarifying with me, asking whether it is all right to have more than one passenger on the same device.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I am certain that I am not the only MP in this House who has received such feedback.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the heart of this feedback, I can understand the anxiety and concern for the wider community.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But beyond supporting this Bill, I have three broad clarifications and concerns.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The first is on how do we ensure a high compliance with this new regulation.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While the intent of the Bill is definitely a positive one, it is worth noting that for someone who wants to be able to ride a mobility scooter, there are a few hurdles for them to cross.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, for those that are not exempted, such as those who are slightly below 70, the first hurdle that they would have to clear is having a valid Certificate of Medical Need to use a mobility scooter on public paths.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The fact that time and effort is required to make an appointment, to find a doctor or occupational therapist who could assess and issue the certification; then, they have to pay for the consultation.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These are hurdles that individuals who need mobility scooters have to cross.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If this process is not implemented well, it may deter people who genuinely need a mobility scooter.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Medical certification aside, individuals who need a mobility scooter will also need to cross another hurdle, which is registering and waiting for the approval of their PMA.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In the event that the individual is still using a non-UL2272 e-scooter, time and resources will be required to find a compliant e-scooter.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My main point is this: if we put ourselves in the user journey, it appears that there are a few hurdles that they will have to go through.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Furthermore, if you happen to be a senior who is just slightly below 70 years old, and happen to be not fluent in English and perhaps not great at navigating the online space to register your mobility scooter, your user journey will end up to be significantly longer than expected as you have to rely on the goodwill of others to help you through this process.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, I hope that the implementation of this Bill will take into account these anticipated challenges and hopefully, prioritise the user experience by keeping the process as straightforward and simple as possible.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It should not only be made available in English, but in all other official languages.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Beyond the digital space and in light of the target population that I have just mentioned, there is a need to roll out information on this policy shift using physical materials placed at face-to-face touchpoints such as our polyclinics, community centres or even general practitioner (GP) clinics.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I know we are serious about implementing this, but I hope that we will be able to reduce the friction involved in navigating the compliance process.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the end of day, we want to ensure that our vulnerable populations who need the mobility scooters will not be deterred by the process.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With this in mind, the Government should consider how financial support and aid will be operationalised in the active mobility compliance context.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, whether there will be means-tested assistance and transitional support for those who are moving from non-compliant devices?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, would the Ministry of Transport (MOT) or LTA be able to share details on when and who can qualify for such financial assistance and the extent of financial assistance so that those who need this more will have this assurance that we are designing this with them in mind?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Beyond financial means, allow me to speak further a little bit about the medical certification.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Presently, the use of NEHR is only limited to specific purposes or circumstances.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: MOH should also perhaps consider allowing NEHR access to streamline the certification of need.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And what this means is that for our seniors, they can just go to the Active Ageing Centre, find a staff who can help them to navigate through the process, generate the medical certification that they need if they have already met the criteria.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the heart of it, we want to make compliance smooth, not difficult.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If the perceived expected costs incurred in terms of time and effort are too significant, compliance will be challenging.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In order to ensure that compliance within speed limits and good behaviour with mobility vehicles on footpaths, the certainty of enforcement plays an important role.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If not, to the mobility vehicle user, this new speed limit is really nothing more than just head knowledge and may not be taken into heart.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Against this backdrop, I wonder how can we ensure enforcement will be more effective.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This could include targeted pilots using speed detection sensors, camera-supported enforcement and other pragmatic tools.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It could involve working closely with Home Team technology partners, including the Home Team Science and Technology Agency so that detection and responses can become faster and more consistent.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A good thing is this: in Singapore, we fortunately have a strong foundation to build on.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, given our extensive Police Camera (PolCam) network deployed across neighbourhoods and transport nodes, this raises a practical question of whether we can leverage on the camera infrastructure and analytics to identify wrong behaviour more quickly, such as speeding of mobility vehicles or even pillion riders on mobility scooters, so that we can ensure enforcement can be carried out more swiftly.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Beyond enforcement, our behaviour is also shaped by our infrastructure.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Just as vehicles drive on roads, where we often have speed limits to remind us drivers of what are the permissible speeds, could we also do something similar for our mobility vehicle users?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The broader question is really how do we ensure that the education of this new speed limit is not just one-off, but repeated periodically and ingrained into our behaviour?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because for many of these residents, mobility vehicles are not a lifestyle choice.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If the new regulatory regime is perceived as one that is making daily living more difficult, more stigmatising, more uncertain, then compliance will be a lot harder and the policy intent may not be fully achieved.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In one of my recent house visits, two of my residents who are wheelchair-bound and they use mobility vehicles to get around, raised a valid concern and I hope the Ministry can give some assurance to this.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: One of these residents mentioned to me saying that if she were to be travelling at six kilometres per hour upslope, their fear is that they will roll backwards given the slower speed.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: From a layman’s perspective as she was sharing that during my house visit, I could understand why she raised this concern, because it is quite easy to conflate two concepts, power and velocity, together.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, what I then did was I raised this concern with my volunteers at my Meet-the-People Session and my Clementi running group.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We sat down together using concepts we learnt from physics and engineering, we drew a free body diagram to simulate whether this concern is valid.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Using our very simple physics model, the motors of the mobility vehicle must be able to overcome the downhill component gravity of mg sin θ.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Another concern is the issue of being unfairly judged or confronted.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some have shared that they fear being stopped or challenged in public, not because they have done anything wrong, but because they “do not look disabled”.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This has been highlighted by disability advocates and rightly so because disability comes in many forms.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, some users can still walk a short distance but rely on mobility aid intermittently.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Ultimately, this Bill is more than just enforcement, it is about how we live together in a dense, compact city with shared spaces.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A "we first" transport culture must mean that pedestrians feel safe.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It also means that legitimate mobility aid users also feel respected and supported.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Our safety rules must not only be stated but enforced consistently, supported with the right resources and technology, applied with fairness so that vulnerable users are not priced out of mobility.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Hoe, we have some students from St Hilda's Secondary School and from their looks I think your calculations are correct.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: It is so important that despite my broken voice today, I wish to share my thoughts, my residents' thoughts on this Bill to ensure safer paths for all.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The growth in the use of PMAs in Singapore shows how our city has evolved – from an ageing population with greater needs for independence to a broader expectation that our public spaces accommodate different forms of mobility.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: But as PMAs become a common sight, it is our duty to strike the right balance of safety, clarity and responsibility between the different users of our public paths.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: On this Bill, I have a few clarifications regarding the enforceability and impact of these new measures.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: First, focusing on the most impacted group: the PMA users.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Given that these PMA users would need the vehicle for basic mobility, the AMS should and must remain affordable for all.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will MOT be coordinating with MOH and the Ministry of Social and Family Development to ensure accessibility and affordability of these services by public and private GPs and occupational therapists that can offer AMS for existing and also new PMA users?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be a fee cap to avoid opportunistic price hiking to obtain the AMS?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: As users’ medical conditions change over time, it is important to ensure PMA users continue to be fit to operate PMAs to reduce the likelihood of accidents.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Assessment to Own does not mean Assessment to Operate.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen some PMA users, while medically allowed to own a PMA, may not have the ability to safely operate their devices and this jeopardises other path users.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: PMA users should meet baseline requirements of eyesight, dexterity and mental state to safely operate their devices.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This may also change with time if health conditions worsen or simply from ageing.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be a validity of each AMS to ensure continued assessment on safe riding of PMAs?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: For example, a reassessment once every three years for those with severe chronic conditions.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the effectiveness of the regulations in making our footpaths and roads safer for everyone.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: There may have been much much more accidents that went unreported.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The new regulations aim to reduce accidents involving pedestrians due to reckless speeding on footpaths and shared paths.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: However, the prevalence of motorised PMA users might make it difficult to enforce penalties against many cases, with some riders who decide to hit and run after the collision to avoid punishment.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Most will comply but there may still be recalcitrant users who disregard the rules.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry consider establishing a demerit system for PMA users to deter repeat offenders who fail to consider the safety of others?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will there be physical features installed, similar to red light cameras on the roads, on shared paths to track speed limits?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: There are still some confusion on regulations surrounding active mobility vehicles such as the speed limit and which paths or roads each vehicle is allowed to ride on.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Just as we are getting used to the terms of PMA, PMD and PAB, we are now hearing new terms from the Ministry – motorised vehicles, motorised wheelchairs, motorised scooters.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry consider increasing better and fuller public communications efforts, such as placing visible signages on speed limits and designating which vehicles are allowed on footpaths, shared paths and roads?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This will reduce the number of accidents due to some riders and pedestrians who unintentionally use the wrong paths.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, which I think has been highlighted in this Chamber by some Members, there are other factors other than speed that pose safety risks and public disturbance.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, you hear them before you see them.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Some active mobility users play loud music on their devices, almost like a mobile disco blasting through the Housing and Development Board (HDB) blocks and footpaths.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: And sometimes, during wee hours of the night.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Ministry look into restricting the playing of loud music on such devices to minimise disturbance and to show consideration for the community?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The new regulations on speed limit and vehicle registration are likely to result in loss of income for many delivery riders who depend on the device for their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Has the Ministry consulted with major food delivery platforms on changes in compensation structures or job allocations due to the new regulations?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This could include allocating shorter distance deliveries to more PMA delivery riders to mitigate potential fall in earnings.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Or will there be career transition assistance for those who wish to switch out of their delivery jobs?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, delivery riders who switch to PABs or PMDs would not be able to legally ride on pedestrian paths, making it challenging for them to complete their deliveries in HDB estates.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: So, those who do so illegally might pose an even greater risk to pedestrians due to the higher speed limit.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, could the Minister or the Ministry share on plans to improve last mile connectivity by increasing the accessibility of shared paths network within the HDB estates?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the use of Personal Mobility Aids (PMAs) has become increasingly common, and we have a responsibility to balance the safety, responsibility and clarity for all users on public paths.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I hope MOT can further clarify the impact of this Bill on PMA users, road users and food delivery workers, as well as how the new measures can be enforced.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: These users often depend on assistive devices for basic mobility, so this assessment must be affordable for them.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, the health condition of PMA users changes over time.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: They must be fit enough to operate mobility aids to reduce the likelihood of accidents.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Even if they are assessed to own, does not mean they have the ability to operate.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, users must meet basic requirements for vision, dexterity and mental state to safely operate assistive devices.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: For example, patients with serious chronic conditions might undergo reassessment every three years?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I believe most users will comply with regulations, but for those bad actors who repeatedly ignore advice, will the MOT consider implementing a demerit point system as a deterrent to ensure others' safety?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will the authorities consider installing speed detectors on footpaths, similar to enhanced speed cameras and traffic cameras on roads?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, regarding the livelihoods of food delivery workers.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In 2019, after PMDs were banned from footpaths, some delivery workers switched to using PMAs.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The new speed and registration regulations will likely cause delivery workers, who depend on these devices for livelihoods, to lose their income.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: During the transition period, they desperately need additional support.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Will delivery workers who want to change careers receive employment assistance?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Delivery workers who switch to PABs and PMDs will not be able to use pedestrian-only paths, causing difficulties when delivering in HDB estates.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister reveal what plans there are to improve the convenience and connectivity network of shared paths in HDB estates?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: With our rapidly ageing population, mobility aids will only become more prevalent.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I hope this Bill can ensure that all Singaporeans can use our roads safely and conveniently. : Mr Speaker, Sir, notwithstanding these clarifications, I fully support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: With the increasing prevalence of PMA use in our ageing population, I hope that this Bill enables safer and more accessible roads and paths for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many of my residents rely on PMAs to move around their estates safely and independently.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For them, these devices are not a convenience, but an essential part of daily life.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My residents want safer paths and fewer fires in our HDB blocks, but they also want a transport environment that is safe and inclusive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support the Ministry's intent to tighten regulations, but legislation is only as effective as its implementation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When we move from policy papers to the pavements in our estates, the "how" becomes just as important as the "what".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With that in mind, I would like to raise four clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have witnessed seemingly young and able-bodied individuals speeding on mobility scooters, treating them as casual transport.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This endangers pedestrians and undermines confidence in genuine PMA use.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, for many of my elderly residents, a mobility scooter is a lifeline.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is the difference between being confined at home and being able to buy groceries or meet friends.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are residents in their 50s or 60s who may not meet a strict clinical definition of being unable to walk, but who suffer from chronic pain, arthritis or joint degeneration.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may manage short distances within their flats but cannot walk several hundred metres to essential amenities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, mobility needs are not always permanent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some residents may require PMAs immediately after surgery or injury but later recover sufficiently.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This raises important questions about how "temporary" medical need is defined and managed in a way that is fair, clear and not open to abuse.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Related to this, how will the system manage the point at which a temporary medical need ends?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will they be assigned a deadline where they are expected to stop using the PMA?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Must they undergo reassessment if their mobility issues persist beyond the expected recovery period, in order to continue using it?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister assure us that residents will not be left house-bound while waiting for certification?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: During the initial rollout, will enforcement officers prioritise helping residents comply rather than penalising them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, regarding digital inclusion, how does a non-tech-savvy senior who falls just below the age exemption prove their status?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If verification relies on digital platforms, we risk creating anxiety.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I acknowledge the Ministry's efforts to reduce compliance burden through retailer-led registration for new devices and a phased transition for existing users.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, residents fear that honest mistakes may be treated as offences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, if a retailer makes a registration error, will the resident using the device in good faith bear the penalty?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can such errors be resolved simply, especially for seniors who may not have full documentation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, can the Minister clarify the costs involved?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For low-income seniors, even modest fees can be a barrier.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, are there implications for public rental tenants regarding insurance or tenancy rules?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure registration does not disadvantage vulnerable residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, with rules phasing in until 2029, how will residents be clearly and repeatedly informed of what applies at each stage?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many fires occur while devices are being charged at home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, we must distinguish between willful offenders and residents who simply do not know how to dispose of old devices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If disposal is difficult, residents will hide these devices, keeping the risk inside the home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Any disposal framework should focus squarely on safe and accessible removal of unsafe devices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Seniors cannot transport heavy devices to distant e-waste points.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Town Council-level collection drives and bulky-item removal services will be essential and has to be supported by sustained public education.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A suggestion is to have all PMA device listings and categories to come with an advisory on compliant models and make it a reportable offence if the seller mislabels an illegal or modified vehicle as one that is compliant.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, how will the agency combat sales through messaging platforms, like Telegram?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, will the Ministry work with the Ministry of National Development to designate charging or parking spaces in suitable locations, such as void decks?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could minimise the risk of PMAs being parked or charged in corridors or lift lobbies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents are frustrated by fast-moving riders, but they want calmer paths, not just more summonses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support deeming platform operators as employers for liability, but liability alone may not change behaviour.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, how do we prevent contractual distancing, where platforms shift blame to riders without changing operational pressures?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, why does the Bill not explicitly require training or delivery-time management, including algorithmic changes that do not reward speed at the expense of safety?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, will success be measured by reduced accidents and complaints, or simply by enforcement numbers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, will enforcement data be used to redesign recurring conflict hotspots in estates?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And fifth, will platforms share anonymised data to support safer estate planning?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: More broadly, I must raise a concern about enforcement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many of these rules are sound on paper, but enforcement on the ground may be inconsistent and unpredictable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Errant users learn when and where to avoid officers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Only when enforcement is visible, consistent and credible will behaviour truly change.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, even well-designed laws risk becoming paper tigers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These disruptions were avoidable and they underline why prevention and enforcement matter.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In such incidents, it is not just the user who pays the price.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some families even lose beloved pets, or in the worst case scenario, their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This brings us to the heart of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On mandatory registration, accountability must be paired with fairness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And on delivery riders and enforcement, safety must be real on the ground, not just written in law.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill matters because safety is not an abstract concept.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is the quiet confidence of a senior walking home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is the assurance that a charging device will not put homes and livelihoods at risk.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is the belief that shared spaces belong to all of us and must protect the most vulnerable amongst us.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They are asking for rules that are firm, but fair.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For enforcement that is real, consistent and visible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But laws alone do not make communities safe.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we choose compassion alongside enforcement, clarity alongside regulation and care alongside accountability, the measure of this Bill will not be found in the number of offences recorded.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will be found in fewer fires; in safer footpaths; in the vulnerable amongst us, who can move through their estates without fear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And for residents in Yio Chu Kang and for all Singaporeans across this island, that is not just good policy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is the kind of society we are building together.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I focus my remarks on one central issue: how technology can allow us to manage traffic more intelligently, beyond relying primarily on pricing.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our road network cannot expand indefinitely and there are many competing demands on land – we need more housing, more parks, more cycling paths and so forth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For decades, ERP has been one of our levers for managing congestion.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But as technology advances, the question is no longer how much we price road usage, but how intelligently we manage traffic as an integrated system.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ERP 2.0 is often framed as a pricing upgrade, but this framing understates its broader potential.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At its core, ERP 2.0 is also a data and sensing platform.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The new OBUs generate richer, more granular and real-time data – both for motorists and the LTA.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This creates an opportunity to move beyond passive congestion pricing towards active traffic management.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Internationally, cities are already using real-time flow data to dynamically manage their road networks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In London, for example, the Split Cycle Offset Optimisation Technique (SCOOT) system uses live data from sensors and cameras to adjust traffic light timings.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This increases green time in congested corridors and eases bottlenecks without expanding road usage.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Drawing on such precedents, ERP 2.0 data can be integrated with adaptive traffic signal systems, incident responses and corridor-level optimisation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Real-time congestion data can enable more responsive traffic light timings, improve directional flow during peak periods and allow faster interventions at known choke points.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Beyond day-to-day operations, ERP 2.0 data also offers a powerful planning tool.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of expanding roads broadly, planners and engineers can use longitudinal flow data to identify where capacity is genuinely constrained and where it is under-utilised.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such data can show which junctions, rather than entire corridors, are the true bottlenecks; and which lanes are consistently under-used and could be reallocated to other users, such as pedestrians and cyclists.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This enables a shift from broad-based expansion to targeted, data-driven interventions, where minor redesigns, signal adjustments or directional changes could outperform the construction of new roads.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The same flow data can also be used to improve outcomes for public transport users, particularly bus commuters.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ERP 2.0 data can support bus lane prioritisation, by identifying corridors where buses experience the most delays; better route design, based on actual congestion and demand patterns; transfer optimisation, improving coordination between bus services and MRT nodes; last mile connectivity planning, by highlighting short but congested links that disproportionately affect bus reliability.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By embedding these insights into planning and operations, ERP 2.0 can directly enhance bus punctuality, reliability and journey times – strengthening public transport as an attractive and dependable choice.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The shift to virtual gantries under ERP 2.0 offers flexibility and reduces physical clutter.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, international experience suggests that flexibility must be accompanied by clear principles and guardrails.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Early feedback on OBUs has raised concerns around aesthetics, usability and power consumption.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Specific vehicle types or older car models face technical difficulties powering the OBU, given that it requires more energy than the previous In-vehicle Unit (IU).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With regard to user experience issues, other cities have addressed similar challenges through iterative design improvements and structured feedback loops.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Seoul, for instance, smart mobility systems were rolled out alongside continuous refinements, with user satisfaction explicitly tracked as a performance indicator.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And beyond familiarity over time, what new features are planned to ensure ERP 2.0 becomes genuinely more intuitive and useful for motorists?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Turning to active mobility, the Bill strengthens penalties and enforcement powers, particularly for PMAs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is important for safety, but enforcement capacity must be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cities, such as Paris and Amsterdam, increasingly rely on camera-based and automated enforcement to ensure consistent compliance without excessive manpower demands.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Camera-based enforcement enables round-the-clock monitoring, unlike manpower-based enforcement, which relies on occasional checks and predictable hotspots due to inherent resource constraints.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Leveraging technology in this way allows enforcement to scale with usage while maintaining fairness and predictability.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From time to time, my residents in Zhenghua have been asking me whether certain types of PMA users should, in fact, be using PMAs, as some appear young and healthy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A certifiable medical requirement helps remove such suspicions and ambiguity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is essential to foster trust and social acceptance within our community.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, I wish to raise an issue of equity and access.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some PMA users come from lower-income households and even small administrative costs can become a barrier.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One that uses data to optimise traffic flow, guide infrastructure planning, improve public transport reliability and enhance user experience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cities around the world show that pricing works best when paired with real-time traffic management, adaptive control and thoughtful use of data.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope Singapore will continue to lead in this space, not just by pricing roads efficiently, but by managing them intelligently.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are the lived realities and anxieties of residents, workers, caregivers and persons with mobility challenges whom we meet on the ground every day.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These views reflect a consolidated position of the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Transport and fellow People's Action Party Members, shaped through extensive discussions within the Committee, engagements with Members and most importantly, direct feedback from residents across our constituencies who will feel the full impact of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Taken together, the GPC's views rest on three clear and urgent concerns.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, Members strongly support safety as the central objective of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Safer paths, safer roads and safer homes are not optional – they are essential.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Residents want assurance that injuries, misuse, fires and unsafe modifications linked to increasingly powerful devices will be decisively addressed.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, they expect safety measures, such as speed limiters, tougher penalties for dangerous alterations and smarter traffic management systems to deliver real, visible improvements on the ground, not just rules on paper.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For many genuine users, those with temporary injuries, functional mobility challenges, caregiving duties or delivery riders relying on mobility aids for their livelihood, the Bill is not theoretical.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It affects whether they can move, work or live with dignity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Third, Members emphasise the success of this Bill will ultimately be judged on enforcement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Residents are asking for enforcement that is consistent, credible and fair – not sporadic crackdowns or uneven treatment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This means sustained enforcement on the ground, better use of technology and clear accountability for platforms and marketplaces that profit from the usage and sales of these devices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The GPC supports the intent of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We offer these views to ensure that implementation is firm yet fair, strong yet compassionate, so that safety is enhanced without losing sight of inclusivity and lived realities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Please allow me to address their comments on the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)-related amendments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked about the regulatory and enforcement approach for foreign-registered heavy vehicles, vis-à-vis Singapore-registered heavy vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Speed limiters are employed upstream to reduce the speeding risk before the offence occurs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore-registered heavy vehicles account for the bulk of daily heavy vehicle traffic on our roads.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Installing speed limiters for these vehicles would therefore reduce the road safety risks associated with heavy vehicles very significantly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We also recognise the need to address the safety risks associated with foreign-registered heavy vehicles.
